You need the results to appear on the Tests tab of each pipeline run. You add the following step:

- task: PublishTestResults@2
  inputs:
    testResultsFormat: SLOT_1
    testResultsFiles: 'test-results/TEST-*.xml'

Which value should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: JUnit
XUnit
VSTest
NUnit

explanation_html:
Correct answer: JUnit

The --junitxml switch makes pytest write a JUnit-style XML report. PublishTestResults@2 supports JUnit, NUnit, VSTest (TRX), XUnit (xUnit 2) and CTest. The format you choose must match the file, not the language. The JUnit format works with many runners, including pytest and PHPUnit.

XUnit is incorrect because it means the xUnit.net v2 XML schema (assemblies/assembly/collection/test), not the JUnit schema that pytest writes.

VSTest is incorrect because it means the Visual Studio TRX format (*.trx).

NUnit is incorrect because it means the NUnit 2/3 result schemas, which pytest doesn't produce.

References:

  • PublishTestResults@2 - Publish Test Results v2 task

question_html:
Contoso has a YAML pipeline that runs integration tests with a custom script and then publishes the results with PublishTestResults@2. Last week someone renamed the output folder of the test script. Since then, every run has completed as Succeeded with no test results attached, because the task found no files that match the testResultsFiles pattern.

You need the pipeline to fail when no test result files are found.

Solution: You set failTaskOnFailedTests: true on the PublishTestResults@2 task.

Does this meet the goal?

options.text: Yes
No

explanation_html:
Correct answer: No

failTaskOnFailedTests fails the task only when the result files that were found contain failed tests. If no files match, there are no failed tests to evaluate, so the task still succeeds.

To meet the goal, set failTaskOnMissingResultsFile: true. It fails the task when no result files are found, and its default is false. The related input failTaskOnFailureToPublishResults fails the task when publishing fails.

References:

  • PublishTestResults@2 - Publish Test Results v2 task

question_html:
Fabrikam runs Maven tests for a Java service in Azure Pipelines and generates a JaCoCo XML coverage report. The pipeline publishes it with this step:

- task: PublishCodeCoverageResults@2
  inputs:
    summaryFileLocation: '$(System.DefaultWorkingDirectory)/service/target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml'

The Code Coverage tab shows the coverage percentages, but you can't open source files to see which lines are covered.

What should you add to the task?

options.text: pathToSources: '$(System.DefaultWorkingDirectory)/service/src/main/java/'
failIfCoverageEmpty: true
codeCoverageTool: 'JaCoCo'
reportDirectory: '$(System.DefaultWorkingDirectory)/service/target/site/jacoco'

explanation_html:
Correct answer: pathToSources

JaCoCo reports don't contain absolute paths to source files. PublishCodeCoverageResults@2 needs pathToSources to point to the source root on the agent (for example .../src/main/java/) to map coverage to source files. This input is also used when tests run inside a Docker container.

failIfCoverageEmpty is incorrect because it only fails the task when no coverage results exist. Here, results are already being published.

codeCoverageTool and reportDirectory are incorrect because they are inputs of the older PublishCodeCoverageResults@1 task. Version 2 has only summaryFileLocation, pathToSources and failIfCoverageEmpty, and it accepts many coverage formats without a tool setting.

References:

  • PublishCodeCoverageResults@2 - Publish code coverage results v2 task

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank hosts its code in Azure Repos Git. A YAML pipeline named payments-ci runs on every pull request to main. It runs the tests and publishes coverage with PublishCodeCoverageResults@2.

You need to meet the following requirements:

  • At least 80% of the lines added or changed in a pull request must be covered by tests.
  • A pull request that doesn't meet this target must be blocked from completing.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Add an azurepipelines-coverage.yml file to the root of the repository that sets coverage.status.diff.target to 80%.
Add a required status check branch policy on main for the code coverage status that the payments-ci pipeline posts.
Set failIfCoverageEmpty: true on the PublishCodeCoverageResults@2 task.
Add a VSTest@3 task with runOnlyImpactedTests: true so that only changed code is measured.
Set the build validation policy on main to Optional so that the coverage result is shown on the pull request.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Add azurepipelines-coverage.yml with a diff target of 80%, and add a required status check policy for the coverage status.

Diff coverage measures only the lines changed in a pull request. Its default target is 70%. You change the target in a file named azurepipelines-coverage.yml at the repository root, for example:

coverage:
  status:
    diff:
      target: 80%

By default, the coverage status posted to the pull request is advisory only. To block merges that miss the target, configure a branch policy that requires the status check. The status is named after the pipeline ({pipeline-name}/codecoverage).

failIfCoverageEmpty is incorrect because it only fails the task when no coverage data exists. It doesn't enforce a percentage.

runOnlyImpactedTests is incorrect because Test Impact Analysis chooses which tests to run. It doesn't measure or enforce coverage of changed lines.

An optional build validation policy is incorrect because making the build optional doesn't add a coverage threshold. The block comes from the required coverage status check.

References:

  • Review and configure code coverage results in Azure Pipelines
  • PublishCodeCoverageResults@2 - Publish code coverage results v2 task

question_html:
Northwind Traders is adopting a shift-left test strategy based on the L0–L4 test taxonomy in the Microsoft DevOps guidance. A team has a test that does the following:

  • Loads the order-processing assembly.
  • Reads and writes rows in a local SQL Server instance.
  • Doesn't need a deployed instance of the service.

The team wants this test to run before code is merged, together with the other tests at the same level.

How should you classify the test?

options.text: L2 – a functional test that needs the assembly plus dependencies such as SQL or the file system
L0 – a fast, in-memory unit test
L3 – a functional test that runs against a testable service deployment
L4 – an integration test that runs against production

explanation_html:
Correct answer: L2

In the taxonomy, L0 and L1 tests depend only on the code in the assembly under test. L2 tests are functional tests that may need the assembly plus other dependencies, such as SQL or the file system. L3 tests need a testable service deployment, and L4 tests run against production. This test uses SQL Server but no deployment, so it's L2. In the guidance's example, developers run L2 tests before they commit.

L0 is incorrect because L0 tests are in-memory and depend on nothing outside the assembly under test.

L3 is incorrect because L3 needs a deployed instance of the service, which this test doesn't use.

L4 is incorrect because L4 tests need a full production deployment.

References:

  • Shift testing left with unit tests

question_html:
Adatum runs about 4,000 MSTest tests in Azure Pipelines (Azure DevOps Services) by using the VSTest@3 task. Some UI tests fail at random and then pass when they run again, which causes many failed CI runs.

You need to meet the following requirements:

  • Tests that fail and then pass in the same run must be identified as flaky automatically.
  • Failures of flaky tests must not fail the pipeline, but the tests must still be visible for troubleshooting.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: In Project settings > Test management, turn on flaky test detection with system detection, and set the flaky test options so that flaky tests aren't included in the test summary (pass percentage).
Set rerunFailedTests: true on the VSTest@3 task.
Set continueOnError: true on the VSTest@3 step.
Set failTaskOnFailedTests: false on a PublishTestResults@2 task that runs after VSTest@3.
Set runOnlyImpactedTests: true on the VSTest@3 task.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Turn on flaky test management with system detection, exclude flaky tests from the summary, and turn on rerunFailedTests.

System detection marks a test as flaky when it fails and then passes on a rerun in the same pipeline execution. This works closely with the VSTest task, which reruns failed tests when rerunFailedTests is on (up to rerunMaxAttempts attempts). In Project settings > Test management, you can choose not to include flaky tests in the test summary. Flaky tests are then removed from the pass percentage and listed under Tests not reported. They don't fail the pipeline, but they remain visible with the Flaky tag.

continueOnError is incorrect because it hides every test failure, including real regressions, and doesn't identify flaky tests.

failTaskOnFailedTests: false is incorrect because VSTest@3 publishes results and fails on test failures on its own. That input only applies to the separate publish task, and it doesn't detect flakiness.

runOnlyImpactedTests is incorrect because Test Impact Analysis reduces which tests run. It doesn't detect or suppress flaky tests.

References:

  • Manage flaky tests
  • VSTest@3 - Visual Studio Test v3 task

question_html:
Litware has three test suites that run in Azure Pipelines by using the Visual Studio Test task:

  • Suite1: MSTest unit tests for a .NET Framework 4.8 class library. The tests and code run on the build agent.
  • Suite2: xUnit tests for a .NET 8 (.NET Core) web API.
  • Suite3: Selenium tests that run on the agent against a web app deployed to a separate Azure VM.

You plan to use Test Impact Analysis (TIA) to run only the tests affected by each commit.

Which suites can use TIA without custom dependency mappings?

options.text: Suite1 only
Suite1 and Suite2 only
Suite1 and Suite3 only
Suite1, Suite2, and Suite3

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Suite1 only

TIA works through the Visual Studio Test task (runOnlyImpactedTests). It supports managed .NET Framework code in a single-machine topology, where the tests and the app under test run on the same machine. Suite1 fits these requirements.

Suite2 isn't supported because .NET Core is listed as an unsupported TIA scenario.

Suite3 isn't supported because the tests exercise an app on a different machine (multi-machine topology). You could extend TIA with a custom XML dependency map (TIA.UserMapFile), but the question rules that out.

References:

  • Use Test Impact Analysis

question_html:
Wingtip Toys has a slow regression suite of 12 MSTest assemblies. Many test classes use ClassInitialize and AssemblyInitialize to set up shared state. You change the test job to run on four agents:

jobs:
- job: Regression
  strategy:
    parallel: 4
  steps:
  - task: VSTest@3
    inputs:
      testSelector: testAssemblies
      testAssemblyVer2: '**\*Tests.dll'
      distributionBatchType: SLOT_1

You need to make sure that tests which share initialization state always run on the same agent.

Which value should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: basedOnAssembly
basedOnExecutionTime
basedOnTestCases
customBatchSize

explanation_html:
Correct answer: basedOnAssembly

When a job uses strategy: parallel, the VSTest task splits the tests into slices across the agents. Slicing by test assembly gives each agent whole assemblies. The documentation recommends this when tests in an assembly have dependencies or use AssemblyInitialize/AssemblyCleanup or ClassInitialize/ClassCleanup.

basedOnExecutionTime is incorrect because it groups tests by past run time and can split one assembly across agents. It's meant for tests that have no dependencies.

basedOnTestCases (the default) is incorrect because it divides the test count evenly across agents, so tests from one assembly can end up on different agents.

customBatchSize is incorrect because it isn't a valid distributionBatchType value. It's an option of batchingBasedOnAgentsOption.

References:

  • Run VSTest tests in parallel
  • VSTest@3 - Visual Studio Test v3 task

question_html:
Contoso runs Playwright UI tests in a YAML pipeline. The same full test suite must run against three browsers: Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. The browser is chosen through a BROWSER variable that the test script reads. The three runs must happen at the same time, and each must publish its own test run.

Which job configuration should you use?

options.text:
strategy:
  matrix:
    chromium:
      BROWSER: chromium
    firefox:
      BROWSER: firefox
    webkit:
      BROWSER: webkit

strategy:
  parallel: 3

strategy:
  maxParallel: 3

pool:
  demands:
  - BROWSER -equals chromium,firefox,webkit

explanation_html:
Correct answer: a matrix strategy with one entry per browser

A matrix creates a copy of the job for each entry, and each copy gets its own variables (here BROWSER). Matrix legs run in parallel unless maxParallel limits them. This is the pattern for testing the same code against different configurations.

parallel: 3 is incorrect because it runs three identical copies of the job. The VSTest task uses those copies to split one test suite across agents. It doesn't run the full suite with a different value in each copy.

maxParallel: 3 on its own is incorrect because maxParallel only limits how many matrix legs run at once. Without a matrix, it creates nothing.

Pool demands are incorrect because demands choose an agent by its capabilities. They don't create several jobs or set variables.

References:

  • jobs.job.strategy definition

question_html:
Fabrikam runs an Azure Load Testing JMeter test from Azure Pipelines by using the AzureLoadTest@1 task. The quality gate for the release is:

  • The 90th percentile response time of all requests must be 500 ms or less.
  • The error rate must be 5% or less.

If either condition isn't met, the load test and the pipeline run must fail. You edit the load test configuration file:

version: v0.1
testId: checkout-load
testPlan: checkout.jmx
engineInstances: 2
failureCriteria:
  SLOT_1

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text:
- p90(response_time_ms) > 500
  - percentage(error) > 5

- p90(response_time_ms) < 500
  - percentage(error) < 5

- avg(response_time_ms) > 500
  - count(error) > 5

- errorPercentage: 5
  - timeWindow: 500

explanation_html:
Correct answer: p90(response_time_ms) > 500 and percentage(error) > 5

A fail criterion describes the condition that fails the test, in the form Aggregate_function(client_metric) condition threshold. A load test fails when at least one criterion evaluates to true. In CI/CD, the workflow run status follows the load test status. response_time_ms supports percentile aggregations such as p90, and error supports percentage with the > operator.

The < conditions are incorrect because they would fail the test when performance is good. Also, percentage(error) supports only >.

avg / count(error) is incorrect because the requirement is a 90th percentile, not an average. Also, count isn't a supported aggregation for the error metric.

errorPercentage / timeWindow is incorrect because these are autoStop settings, which stop a test that is running and incurring cost. They aren't pass/fail criteria.

References:

  • Define load test fail criteria - Azure Load Testing

question_html:
Adatum adds a load test stage to an Azure Pipelines YAML pipeline. The stage uses the AzureLoadTest@1 task with an Azure Resource Manager service connection, and it creates and runs tests in an existing Azure Load Testing resource named alt-prod.

You need to grant the service connection's identity the permissions it needs. The solution must use the principle of least privilege.

Which Azure role should you assign on alt-prod?

options.text: Load Test Contributor
Load Test Reader
Monitoring Contributor
Owner

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Load Test Contributor

Azure Load Testing uses Azure RBAC. To create and run load tests from a CI/CD workflow, you assign the Load Test Contributor role to the service principal behind the service connection, scoped to the load testing resource.

Load Test Reader is incorrect because it can view tests and results but can't create or run them.

Monitoring Contributor is incorrect because it's the role you give the load testing resource's managed identity on app components, so it can read server-side metrics. It doesn't allow running load tests.

Owner is incorrect because it grants far more permissions than needed, including managing access.

References:

  • Manually configure CI/CD for load tests - Azure Load Testing
  • Define load test fail criteria - Azure Load Testing

question_html:
Tailspin Toys uses Azure Test Plans. QA leads tag a test case as Smoke whenever it must be part of the release smoke pass. The test plan must always contain every test case tagged Smoke in the Tailspin\Web area path, including test cases tagged later, without anyone adding them by hand.

Which type of test suite should you create?

options.text: Query-based suite
Requirement-based suite
Static suite
A static suite that contains one requirement-based suite for each user story

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Query-based suite

A query-based suite is filled by a work item query. Test cases that match the query (here, tag Smoke and the area path) are included automatically and stay in sync as work items change. Query-based suites are read-only: to change their contents, you change the query.

Requirement-based suite is incorrect because it's tied to one backlog item and tracks test coverage for that requirement. It doesn't select test cases by tag.

Static suite and the nested option are incorrect because static suites are folders that you maintain by hand. New Smoke test cases wouldn't be added automatically.

References:

  • Create and manage test suites

question_html:
Northwind Traders runs manual tests with Azure Test Plans. Every test case in the Checkout test suite must be run and tracked separately for two environments: Microsoft Edge on Windows 11 and Safari on macOS. You must be able to chart pass/fail results for each environment.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Create configuration variables for Browser and Operating system, and then create two test configurations from their values.
Assign both test configurations to the Checkout test suite.
Clone the Checkout test suite into a second test plan for macOS testing.
Add the tags Edge and Safari to each test case in the suite.
Add a strategy: matrix with a BROWSER variable to the pipeline that runs the manual tests.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Create the configuration variables and test configurations, and assign both configurations to the suite.

A test configuration is a combination of configuration variable values, such as Browser and Operating system. You create the variables first and then the configurations. When you assign several configurations to a test suite, each test case is repeated for each configuration as a separate test point. You can then create a test result chart grouped by Configuration.

Cloning into a second plan is incorrect because it duplicates the test artifacts and splits the reporting. Configurations are the built-in way to cover a test matrix.

Tags are incorrect because tags don't create separate test points, so you can't record a separate outcome for each environment.

A pipeline matrix is incorrect because these are manual tests in Azure Test Plans. A matrix strategy creates parallel pipeline jobs, not test points.

References:

  • Test different configurations
  • Create and manage test plans

question_html:
Contoso wants business users to do exploratory testing of a new web portal in Microsoft Edge. The users have Stakeholder access to the Azure DevOps project. Each user must be able to:

  • Capture annotated screenshots and screen recordings while browsing.
  • Create bugs directly in the Azure DevOps project, with links back to the exploratory session.

The solution must not require more licenses. What should you use?

options.text: The Test & Feedback extension in Connected mode
The Test & Feedback extension in Standalone mode
The Test Runner in Azure Test Plans to run test cases from a test suite
Assign Basic + Test Plans access to each business user and use requirement-based test suites

explanation_html:
Correct answer: The Test & Feedback extension in Connected mode

In Connected mode, the extension signs in to Azure DevOps and connects to the project, which gives end-to-end traceability for the work items created during a session. Users with Stakeholder access can capture feedback and create most work items. Only creating test cases is restricted. Screen recordings are supported in Edge and Chrome.

Standalone mode is incorrect because it doesn't integrate with Azure DevOps. Users can capture data and export a session report, but bugs aren't created in the project.

The Test Runner in Azure Test Plans is incorrect because users with Stakeholder access can't access Azure Test Plans. It also runs scripted test cases, not exploratory sessions.

Basic + Test Plans is incorrect because it adds licenses, which the requirements don't allow.

References:

  • Install the Test & Feedback extension
  • Create and manage test plans

question_html:
Litware enabled Test Impact Analysis on the Visual Studio Test task in its CI pipeline for a .NET Framework solution:

- task: VSTest@3
  inputs:
    testSelector: testAssemblies
    testAssemblyVer2: '**\*UnitTests.dll'
    runOnlyImpactedTests: true
    SLOT_1: '10'

To keep the test-to-code mapping current, the pipeline must run the complete test suite automatically after every 10 builds and run only impacted tests in the other builds.

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: runAllTestsAfterXBuilds
rerunMaxAttempts
minimumExpectedTests
customBatchSizeValue

explanation_html:
Correct answer: runAllTestsAfterXBuilds

When runOnlyImpactedTests is true, runAllTestsAfterXBuilds sets how many builds run before all tests run automatically. The default is 50. TIA stores a mapping between tests and source code, and the documentation recommends running all tests regularly to rebuild that mapping. To force a full run for one build only, you can set the DisableTestImpactAnalysis variable to true.

rerunMaxAttempts is incorrect because it limits how many times failed tests are retried.

minimumExpectedTests is incorrect because it fails the task if fewer tests than the minimum run.

customBatchSizeValue is incorrect because it sets the number of tests per batch when tests are distributed across agents.

References:

  • VSTest@3 - Visual Studio Test v3 task
  • Use Test Impact Analysis

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank exposes a public REST endpoint, https://api.woodgrove.example/health. You need to monitor it from several Azure regions by using Application Insights. The monitoring must:

  • Send an HTTP POST request with a JSON body and a custom X-Probe-Key header.
  • Fail when the TLS certificate is within 14 days of expiring.

The solution must not need code changes to the API. What should you create?

options.text: An Application Insights Standard test with the SSL certificate validity check and proactive lifetime check turned on
An Application Insights URL ping test with content match
A custom availability test that calls TrackAvailability() from an Azure Function
A log search alert rule that queries the requests table for failed POST requests

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A Standard test

Standard tests send a single request to a public endpoint from the test locations you choose. Unlike URL ping tests, they support HTTP verbs such as POST, a custom request body, custom headers, TLS/SSL certificate validity checks, and a proactive lifetime check that fails the test a set number of days before the certificate expires.

URL ping test is incorrect because URL ping tests are deprecated and don't support custom verbs, bodies, headers or certificate lifetime checks.

TrackAvailability() is incorrect because custom availability tests need code that you write and host. The current documentation treats them as archived Classic API guidance and recommends Standard tests where possible.

A log search alert on requests is incorrect because it only sees real traffic that reaches the app. It doesn't probe the endpoint or check certificates.

References:

  • Application Insights availability tests

question_html:
Adatum has an Application Insights Standard test that runs every 5 minutes from five test locations, with retries turned on. Engineers are getting paged when a single test location has a short network issue.

You need to change the availability alert so it fires only for real outages, following Microsoft's recommended relationship between test locations and the alert location threshold.

What alert location threshold should you set?

options.text: 3 of 5 locations
1 of 5 locations
5 of 5 locations
2 of 5 locations

explanation_html:
Correct answer: 3 of 5 locations

The guidance is: alert location threshold = number of test locations - 2, with at least five test locations. Five locations give a threshold of 3, which matches the documented minimum recommendation of 3/5. With this threshold, a problem in one or two locations, such as a network issue, doesn't fire the alert.

1 of 5 is incorrect because a single location failing would page engineers, which is the current problem.

2 of 5 is incorrect because it's below the recommended threshold and still sensitive to local network problems.

5 of 5 is incorrect because a real outage that one location doesn't see would never fire the alert.

References:

  • Application Insights availability tests

question_html:
Fabrikam has a Python web service that sends telemetry to Application Insights through the OpenTelemetry distro and its Azure Monitor exporter. By default, the distro samples traces with a rate limit. You need to keep about 10% of traces instead, so the sampling rate grows with traffic. Sampling must be configured without code changes. You add these app settings:

OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=SLOT_1
OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=SLOT_2

What should you use for SLOT_1 and SLOT_2?

options.text: SLOT_1: microsoft.fixed_percentage; SLOT_2: 0.1
SLOT_1: microsoft.fixed_percentage; SLOT_2: 10
SLOT_1: microsoft.rate_limited; SLOT_2: 0.1
SLOT_1: always_off; SLOT_2: 0.9

explanation_html:
Correct answer: microsoft.fixed_percentage with 0.1

Application Insights supports two sampling strategies with OpenTelemetry: fixed-rate, with a ratio between 0 and 1, and rate-limited, with a maximum number of traces per second. In Python and Node.js, you set them with OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG. For microsoft.fixed_percentage, the argument is a value from 0.0 to 1.0, so 0.1 keeps about 10% of traces.

10 is incorrect because the argument is a ratio, not a percentage.

microsoft.rate_limited with 0.1 is incorrect because rate-limited sampling treats the argument as traces per second, so 0.1 means about one trace every 10 seconds, whatever the traffic.

always_off is incorrect because it drops all traces.

References:

  • Configure OpenTelemetry in Application Insights
  • Sampling in Azure Application Insights with OpenTelemetry

question_html:
Contoso runs three Node.js microservices (cart, catalog and payment) in Azure Container Apps. They are instrumented with the OpenTelemetry distro for Azure Monitor and send telemetry to one Application Insights resource. In Application Map, the services don't appear as separate nodes, so engineers can't follow distributed calls between them.

You need each service to appear as its own node. What should you configure for each service?

options.text: Set the OTEL_SERVICE_NAME environment variable (the service.name resource attribute) to a different value for each service.
Give each service its own APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING that points to a separate Application Insights resource.
Set the service.instance.id resource attribute to the container replica name.
Turn on ingestion sampling at 100% on the Application Insights resource.

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Set OTEL_SERVICE_NAME / service.name for each service

Application Map labels each node with the Cloud Role Name. With OpenTelemetry, the Cloud Role Name comes from the service.namespace and service.name resource attributes, or from service.name alone. You can set these with OTEL_SERVICE_NAME and OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES. A distinct name for each service gives a distinct node, and the correlated dependency calls are drawn between the nodes.

Separate Application Insights resources is incorrect because it splits telemetry and adds work. It isn't the way to name components within one map.

service.instance.id is incorrect because it sets the Cloud Role Instance, the replica or host, not the role name shown on the node.

Ingestion sampling is incorrect because it only controls how much telemetry is kept, not how components are identified.

References:

  • Configure OpenTelemetry in Application Insights

question_html:
Tailspin Toys needs two Azure Monitor alerts:

  • Alert1: Fire when the Percentage CPU platform metric of any of 40 VMs in one region stays above 85%, with as little latency as possible. Each VM must get its own notification.
  • Alert2: Fire when more than 20 application exceptions that contain the text PaymentGatewayTimeout are logged in 15 minutes. Finding them requires joining the exceptions and requests tables by operation ID.

Which alert rule type should you use for each alert?

options.text: Alert1: metric alert rule; Alert2: log search alert rule
Alert1: log search alert rule; Alert2: metric alert rule
Alert1: activity log alert rule; Alert2: log search alert rule
Alert1: metric alert rule; Alert2: activity log alert rule

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Alert1 metric alert, Alert2 log search alert

Metric alerts evaluate precomputed metric data that needs little or no manipulation. One metric alert rule can monitor many VMs of the same type in one region and sends a separate notification for each resource. Metric data has less latency than logs.

Log search alerts run a Log Analytics (KQL) query at a set frequency. They are the right choice when the data is in logs or needs advanced logic, such as text filters and joins between tables.

Activity log alerts are incorrect for both. They fire on control-plane events, such as a resource being deleted or a Service Health event, not on performance metrics or application exceptions.

Swapping the types is incorrect because a metric alert can't run a KQL join over exceptions. Using a log search alert for CPU adds latency and cost when the metric is already available.

References:

  • Types of Azure Monitor alerts

question_html:
Northwind Traders has three Azure Monitor alert rules for its production web app. When any of them fires:

  • The same three on-call engineers must get an email and an SMS.
  • A formatted message must be posted to the Prod-Incidents Microsoft Teams channel.

You need a solution that is easy to maintain. Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Create one action group that has email and SMS notifications for the three engineers, and associate it with all three alert rules.
Add a Logic Apps action to the action group that posts the alert to the Teams channel.
Create a separate action group for each alert rule, each with the same three engineers.
Add a Webhook action that points directly to the Teams channel's incoming webhook URL and expects the Teams message schema.
Use the Email Azure Resource Manager role notification type with the Reader role to reach the three engineers.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: One shared action group, and a Logic Apps action for Teams.

An action group is defined by its set of actions and recipients. Several alert rules can use the same action group, so one group for the three engineers is the easiest to maintain. To post to Microsoft Teams, Microsoft recommends a Logic Apps action, which can turn the alert payload into a Teams message.

Separate action groups for each rule is incorrect because it repeats the same configuration three times.

A direct Webhook to Teams is incorrect because a webhook action sends the alert JSON payload. If the target expects a specific schema, such as the Teams schema, the documentation says to use a Logic Apps action to transform it.

Email ARM role (Reader) is incorrect because it emails everyone with that role on the subscription, not only the three engineers, and it doesn't send SMS.

References:

  • Create and manage action groups in Azure Monitor

question_html:
Contoso wants a dashboard tile that shows the 95th percentile server response time of its API for the last 24 hours, in 15-minute intervals. You write this query in Application Insights Logs:

requests
| where timestamp > ago(24h)
| summarize SLOT_1 by bin(timestamp, 15m)
| render timechart

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: percentile(duration, 95)
percentile(duration, 0.95)
avg(duration)
max(duration) * 0.95

explanation_html:
Correct answer: percentile(duration, 95)

summarize groups rows by its by expressions. Here bin(timestamp, 15m) creates 15-minute buckets, and the aggregation runs once for each bucket. percentile(expr, percentile) estimates the nearest-rank percentile, and the percentile is given on a 0–100 scale, so the 95th percentile is 95.

percentile(duration, 0.95) is incorrect because 0.95 would be the 0.95th percentile, close to the minimum, not the 95th.

avg(duration) is incorrect because an average hides tail latency, which is what a p95 measures.

max(duration) * 0.95 is incorrect because scaling the maximum isn't a percentile and is distorted by single outliers.

References:

  • percentile(), percentiles() - Kusto
  • summarize operator - Kusto

question_html:
Litware's engineering leadership wants to track software delivery performance. A team lead suggests the following measurements:

  • Measure A: The number of deployments of code changes to production each day.
  • Measure B: The percentage of production changes that cause a failure that needs a hotfix or rollback.
  • Measure C: The time from the start of a production incident until service is restored.

Which DevOps (DORA) metric does each measurement represent?

options.text: A: Deployment frequency; B: Change failure rate; C: Mean time to restore (MTTR)
A: Lead time for changes; B: Change failure rate; C: Mean time to restore (MTTR)
A: Deployment frequency; B: Mean time to restore (MTTR); C: Lead time for changes
A: Deployment frequency; B: Defect escape rate; C: Cycle time

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A Deployment frequency, B Change failure rate, C Mean time to restore

The Cloud Adoption Framework lists four software delivery performance metrics. Deployment Frequency is the number of deployments of code changes to production per day. Change Fail Percentage is the percentage of changes to production that lead to a failure. Mean Time to Restore is the time it takes to restore service in production after an incident. Lead Time for Change is the time it takes for a change to go from idea to deployment in production.

Lead time for changes is incorrect for Measure A because lead time measures how long a change takes, not how often you deploy.

MTTR for B / lead time for C is incorrect because B is a percentage of failed changes and C measures recovery, not delivery speed.

Defect escape rate and cycle time are incorrect because they are a quality metric (defects found by end users) and a work-item flow metric, not the delivery measures described here.

References:

  • DevOps considerations - Cloud Adoption Framework

question_html:
Wingtip Toys has a multi-stage YAML pipeline in Azure DevOps Services whose success rate has dropped over the last two weeks. The release manager wants to find, without writing queries or installing extensions:

  • How the pass rate changed day by day, broken down by stage.
  • Which specific tasks cause most of the failed runs, with links to those runs.

What should the release manager use?

options.text: The Pipeline pass rate report on the pipeline's Analytics tab
The Pipeline duration report on the pipeline's Analytics tab
The Test failures report on the pipeline's Analytics tab
The Cumulative Flow Diagram widget on a team dashboard

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Pipeline pass rate report

Pipeline analytics are on the pipeline's Analytics tab. The Pipeline pass rate report has a summary, a failure trend of failures per day (divided by stage when the pipeline has several stages), and a list of top failing tasks and their failed runs. By default it shows the last 14 days, and you can filter by date range and branch.

Pipeline duration report is incorrect because it shows how long successful runs take and the longest tasks, not failures.

Test failures report is incorrect because it lists failing tests, not failing pipeline tasks such as deployment or build steps.

Cumulative Flow Diagram is incorrect because it shows how work items move through board states, not pipeline health.

References:

  • Pipeline reports - Azure Pipelines

question_html:
Adatum deploys a web app with a multi-stage YAML pipeline. The Canary stage deploys to the canary environment, and the Production stage deploys to the production environment. Azure Monitor alert rules watch the canary instance's failure rate and response time.

You need the Production stage to start only when none of those alert rules are firing. Health must be re-evaluated every 10 minutes for up to 1 hour. Pipeline authors must not be able to remove this control by editing the YAML file.

What should you configure?

options.text: A Query Azure Monitor alerts check on the production environment, with Time between evaluations set to 10 minutes and Timeout set to 60 minutes
An AzureMonitor@1 task as the first step of the Production stage's deployment job
A stage condition on the Production stage that evaluates succeeded('Canary')
A Business hours check on the production environment

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A Query Azure Monitor alerts check on the production environment

Approvals and checks are set on protected resources such as environments, not in the YAML file, so pipeline authors can't change them. The Query Azure Monitor alerts check succeeds when no alert rules are active at the time of evaluation, so it can confirm that the canary is healthy before the next stage starts. The check runs again after the Time between evaluations, and the stage doesn't run if the checks don't pass within the Timeout.

A task inside the stage is incorrect because it's defined in YAML, which pipeline authors can edit or remove, and it runs only after the stage has started.

succeeded('Canary') is incorrect because it only checks that the previous stage finished successfully. It doesn't look at the application's health after deployment, and it's also in YAML.

Business hours is incorrect because it controls when a stage can start, not whether the application is healthy.

References:

  • Pipeline deployment approvals (approvals and checks)

question_html:
Contoso has a YAML pipeline in Azure Pipelines. A pipeline variable named ApiKey is defined in the pipeline settings UI with Keep this value secret selected. A Bash step runs ./deploy.sh, which reads the key from the environment variable API_KEY.

steps:
- bash: ./deploy.sh
  displayName: Deploy

During the run, deploy.sh reports that API_KEY is empty. You need to make the key available to the script. The solution must minimize the risk of the key being exposed through process listings or command-line logging.

What should you do?

options.text: Add an env section to the Bash step that maps API_KEY: $(ApiKey)
Change the script line to ./deploy.sh $(ApiKey) and read the key from the first argument
Clear Keep this value secret on the ApiKey variable so that it is mapped to an environment variable automatically
Add a preceding step that runs echo "##vso[task.setvariable variable=API_KEY]$(ApiKey)"

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Add an env section to the Bash step that maps API_KEY: $(ApiKey).

Unlike normal variables, secret variables are not automatically decrypted into environment variables for scripts. You must explicitly map them, and Microsoft recommends mapping secrets into environment variables rather than passing them on the command line, because some operating systems log command-line arguments.

Passing $(ApiKey) as a command-line argument is incorrect because it works functionally but exposes the secret on the command line, which Microsoft explicitly advises against.

Clearing Keep this value secret is incorrect because it removes encryption and log masking for the key, which defeats the purpose of storing it as a secret.

Using task.setvariable without issecret is incorrect because it echoes the secret to standard output, which Microsoft says never to do, and it copies the key into a new non-secret variable. Non-secret variables are automatically exposed as environment variables to every later step and lose the protections of a secret variable, so the exposure is wider than an explicit env mapping on the one step that needs it.

References:

  • Set secret variables - Azure Pipelines

question_html:
Fabrikam stores database credentials for a pipeline as a single secret variable named DbConfig in an Azure Pipelines variable group. The value is a JSON document similar to { "user": "svc-app", "password": "<value>" }. A script step parses the JSON and, while troubleshooting, prints the password property. The password appears in clear text in the pipeline log even though DbConfig is marked as secret.

You need to ensure that the password is masked if it is ever written to the log. What should you do?

options.text: Store the user name and the password as separate secret variables instead of one JSON secret
Move the DbConfig variable from the variable group to the pipeline settings UI and mark it as secret
Set the system.debug variable to false for the pipeline
Mark DbConfig as readonly in the YAML variables section

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Store each sensitive value as its own secret variable.

Azure Pipelines masks the full value of a secret but never masks substrings of a secret. If a secret contains structured data such as JSON, a property value extracted from it (for example bar from { "foo": "bar" }) isn't masked. Microsoft therefore states that secrets should not contain structured data.

Moving the secret to the pipeline settings UI is incorrect because masking behavior is the same wherever the secret is defined; the extracted substring would still not be masked.

Setting system.debug to false is incorrect because debug logging does not control secret masking, and the script explicitly prints the value regardless of verbosity.

Marking the variable readonly is incorrect because readonly prevents later steps from overwriting the variable; it has no effect on log masking.

References:

  • Set secret variables - Azure Pipelines

question_html:
Northwind has a variable group named prod-secrets that is linked to an Azure key vault. The variable group maps the secrets SqlPassword and StorageKey. YAML pipelines reference the group by using - group: prod-secrets.

A security engineer performs the following actions in the key vault:

  • Rotates the value of SqlPassword.
  • Adds a new secret named RedisKey.

The next pipeline run uses the new SqlPassword value, but the $(RedisKey) macro is not resolved. You need to make RedisKey available to the pipelines. What should you do?

options.text: Edit the prod-secrets variable group and add RedisKey to the list of mapped secrets
Grant the service connection the List permission on the key vault
Re-authorize the Azure Resource Manager service connection used by the variable group
Queue the pipeline again after the variable group cache refreshes

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Edit the variable group and add RedisKey to the mapped secrets.

Only secret names are mapped to a Key Vault-linked variable group; values are fetched at run time. Changes to the values of existing secrets are automatically available, which is why the rotated SqlPassword works. However, when secrets are added to or deleted from the vault, the variable group isn't updated automatically. You must explicitly update the secrets included in the variable group.

Granting List permission is incorrect because the service connection already reads the vault successfully (the rotated value is fetched); the issue is that the new secret isn't mapped in the variable group.

Re-authorizing the service connection is incorrect because authorization is not the problem; the variable group simply doesn't contain the new secret name.

Waiting for a cache refresh is incorrect because there is no automatic refresh that adds new vault secrets to the variable group; the change must be made explicitly.

References:

  • Link a variable group to secrets in Azure Key Vault

question_html:
Tailspin Toys has the following job in a YAML pipeline. The key vault contains more than 40 secrets. The job must download only SqlPassword and StorageKey, and both secrets must be available to every step in the job, including steps that appear before the Key Vault task.

steps:
- script: ./prepare.sh
- task: AzureKeyVault@2
  inputs:
    azureSubscription: 'sc-tailspin-prod'
    KeyVaultName: 'kv-tailspin-prod'
    SecretsFilter: SLOT_1
    RunAsPreJob: SLOT_2
- script: ./deploy.sh

How should you complete SLOT_1 and SLOT_2?

options.text: SLOT_1: 'SqlPassword,StorageKey'   SLOT_2: true
SLOT_1: '*'   SLOT_2: true
SLOT_1: 'SqlPassword,StorageKey'   SLOT_2: false
SLOT_1: 'SqlPassword;StorageKey'   SLOT_2: false

explanation_html:
Correct answer: SecretsFilter: 'SqlPassword,StorageKey' and RunAsPreJob: true.

SecretsFilter accepts either the default * (all secrets) or a comma-separated list of secret names. RunAsPreJob (default false) runs the task before the job execution begins and exposes the secrets to all tasks in the job, not just tasks that follow the Key Vault task.

SecretsFilter '*' is incorrect because it downloads every secret in the vault, which violates the requirement to download only two secrets.

RunAsPreJob: false is incorrect because with the default value, secrets are available only to tasks that run after the Key Vault task, so prepare.sh wouldn't receive them.

A semicolon-separated filter with RunAsPreJob false is incorrect because the filter must be comma-separated, and RunAsPreJob false doesn't expose the secrets to earlier steps.

References:

  • AzureKeyVault@2 - Azure Key Vault v2 task

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank uses an Azure key vault that is configured with the Azure role-based access control permission model. Public network access to the vault is disabled, and the vault is reachable only through a private endpoint. Woodgrove needs to create an Azure Pipelines variable group that is linked to secrets in this vault.

Solution: You assign the Key Vault Secrets User role on the vault to the identity of the Azure Resource Manager service connection, and then link the variable group to the vault.

Does this meet the goal?

options.text: Yes
No

explanation_html:
Correct answer: No.

Key vaults that use the RBAC permission model are supported for variable group linking only when the vault is reachable over a public endpoint. RBAC key vaults behind private endpoints aren't supported by Azure DevOps, because private endpoint access for RBAC vaults is available only to Azure trusted services and Azure DevOps isn't currently a trusted service. Microsoft's guidance is to switch the vault's permission model to Vault access policy (granting at least Get and List) if you must use a private endpoint.

Assigning Key Vault Secrets User would be the right role for an RBAC vault with a public endpoint, but it doesn't overcome the private endpoint limitation.

References:

  • Link a variable group to secrets in Azure Key Vault

question_html:
Adatum has several Azure Resource Manager service connections in Azure DevOps that authenticate by using service principal secrets. Pipelines regularly fail when the secrets expire. You plan to use the built-in Convert action in Azure DevOps to switch the connections to workload identity federation.

Which two conditions must a service connection meet to be converted by using the conversion tool? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: The service connection was originally created automatically by Azure DevOps
The service connection is used by only one project
The service connection uses a certificate instead of a client secret
The service connection is scoped to a management group rather than a subscription
The service connection is shared with at least one other project

explanation_html:
Correct answers: The connection was created automatically by Azure DevOps, and it is used by only one project.

The conversion tool works only for service connections that Azure DevOps originally created; manually created connections can't be converted with the tool because Azure DevOps doesn't have permission to modify their credentials. Cross-project (shared) service connections also can't be converted. Converted automatic connections can be reverted within seven days.

Using a certificate is incorrect because the credential type isn't a conversion prerequisite; the tool replaces the secret-based credential with a federated credential.

Management group scope is incorrect because scope level isn't a conversion requirement; automatic WIF connections support subscription, management group, and Machine Learning workspace scopes.

Shared with another project is incorrect because cross-project service connections are explicitly excluded from conversion.

References:

  • Use an Azure Resource Manager service connection

question_html:
Litware is creating a new Azure Resource Manager service connection in Azure DevOps for a production subscription. Company policy requires that the connection does not use any stored secret. The DevOps engineer creating the connection is not allowed to create app registrations in Microsoft Entra ID, but a user-assigned managed identity that has the required Azure role assignments already exists.

Which authentication option should the engineer select?

options.text: Managed identity, connecting to the existing user-assigned managed identity with a workload identity federation credential
App registration (automatic) with workload identity federation
App registration (automatic) with a secret
Agent-assigned managed identity

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Managed identity, which creates a workload identity federation credential on the existing user-assigned managed identity.

Microsoft recommends workload identity federation for ARM service connections because it eliminates secrets and secret management. When you don't have permission to create an app registration, the documented option is to use an existing user-assigned managed identity; Azure DevOps creates the federated credential on that identity.

App registration (automatic) with workload identity federation is incorrect because this option creates a new app registration in Microsoft Entra ID, which the engineer isn't permitted to do.

App registration (automatic) with a secret is incorrect because it stores a client secret, violating the no-secret policy, and it also requires creating an app registration.

Agent-assigned managed identity is incorrect because it is a legacy option kept for backward compatibility that depends on self-hosted agents running on Azure VMs; it isn't the recommended workload identity federation approach.

References:

  • Use an Azure Resource Manager service connection

question_html:
Contoso is creating an Azure Resource Manager service connection that a single YAML pipeline named web-release will use to deploy an App Service app. All resources for the app are in the resource group rg-web-prod. You need to apply the principle of least privilege to the service connection.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Select the rg-web-prod resource group when you create the service connection at the subscription scope level
Leave Grant access permission to all pipelines cleared and authorize only the web-release pipeline
Assign the service connection identity the Contributor role on the subscription so it can create resource groups when needed
Enable Open access for the service connection in the project
Use a publish profile instead of workload identity federation

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Scope the connection to the resource group, and authorize only the pipeline that needs it.

Microsoft recommends scoping Azure service connections only to necessary resources, avoiding broad contributor rights on the entire subscription and choosing a specific resource group. Selecting Grant access permission to all pipelines isn't recommended; instead, authorize each pipeline individually. Pipeline permissions guard against protected resources being used by other pipelines.

Contributor on the subscription is incorrect because it grants far more access than deploying to one resource group requires.

Enabling Open access is incorrect because it allows every pipeline in the project to use the resource, which Microsoft explicitly advises against.

Using a publish profile is incorrect because it is a legacy, non-recommended option; it doesn't improve least privilege compared with a resource group-scoped workload identity federation connection.

References:

  • Use an Azure Resource Manager service connection
  • Secure agents, projects, and containers
  • Pipeline resource security

question_html:
Wingtip Toys deploys to an Azure Pipelines environment named production from several YAML pipelines. Security requires that a stage can deploy to production only if the run was built from main and main has branch protection enabled. Pipeline authors who can edit YAML must not be able to bypass this control.

What should you configure?

options.text: A Branch control check on the production environment that allows refs/heads/main and requires branch protection
A condition on each deployment stage: eq(variables['Build.SourceBranch'], 'refs/heads/main')
A branch policy on main that requires a minimum number of reviewers
A Required template check on the production environment

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A Branch control check on the environment.

Approvals and checks are not defined in the YAML file, so users who modify the pipeline YAML can't change them; resource owners manage them in the web UI. The Branch control check validates that resources in the run come from allowed branches (specified as fully qualified names such as refs/heads/main) and can mandate that those branches have protection enabled.

A YAML stage condition is incorrect because anyone who can edit the YAML can remove or change the condition, so it doesn't meet the bypass requirement.

A branch policy on main is incorrect because it protects how code gets into main but doesn't stop a pipeline run from another branch from deploying to the environment.

A Required template check is incorrect because it enforces that the pipeline extends a specific template; it doesn't validate the source branch.

References:

  • Pipeline deployment approvals
  • Pipeline resource security

question_html:
Adatum's platform team maintains a YAML template named secure-deploy.yml in a central repository. The template injects credential scanning and restricts which tasks can run. You need to ensure that any pipeline that uses the sc-adatum-prod Azure Resource Manager service connection fails before the stage starts unless the pipeline extends from secure-deploy.yml.

What should you configure?

options.text: A Required template check on the sc-adatum-prod service connection
An Approvals check on the sc-adatum-prod service connection with the platform team as approvers
An Evaluate artifact check on the sc-adatum-prod service connection
Pipeline permissions on the sc-adatum-prod service connection that authorize only pipelines in the central repository

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A Required template check on the service connection.

The Required template check enforces that pipelines use a specific YAML template: if the pipeline doesn't extend from the referenced template (repository, ref, and path), the check fails. It is a static check that runs before approvals. Template effectiveness as a security control relies on enforcement through protected resources such as service connections.

An Approvals check is incorrect because it relies on humans to inspect each run and doesn't automatically verify that the pipeline extends the required template.

Evaluate artifact is incorrect because it evaluates container image artifacts against a custom policy and is configured on environments; it doesn't verify template usage.

Pipeline permissions is incorrect because they control which pipelines can use the resource, but an authorized pipeline could still be edited to stop extending the template.

References:

  • Pipeline deployment approvals
  • Templates for security - Azure Pipelines

question_html:
Fabrikam uses an extends template to wrap steps supplied by application teams. For one task supplied by a team, the template must ensure that logging commands from the task can't publish artifacts or upload test results, and that the task can set only a variable named buildVersion through task.setvariable.

Which YAML should the template apply to that task?

options.text:
target:
  commands: restricted
  settableVariables:
  - buildVersion

target:
  commands: restricted
  settableVariables: []

target: host
readonly: true

target:
  commands: any
  settableVariables:
  - buildVersion

explanation_html:
Correct answer: commands: restricted with settableVariables listing buildVersion.

In restricted mode, most agent services available through logging commands, such as uploading artifacts and attaching test results, are unavailable. The setvariable command remains permitted in restricted mode, so you explicitly declare which variables are settable by using settableVariables; a task that tries to set any other variable fails.

settableVariables: [] is incorrect because an empty list disallows all variable setting, so the task couldn't set buildVersion.

target: host with readonly is incorrect because target: host only selects where the step runs, and readonly is a property of variable definitions, not a step restriction.

commands: any is incorrect because it leaves all logging commands, including artifact publishing, available to the task.

References:

  • Templates for security - Azure Pipelines

question_html:
Northwind has an Azure DevOps organization with 12 projects. All pipelines are YAML pipelines. A security review found that a YAML pipeline in one project can clone repositories from every other project in the organization by using the job access token. You need to ensure that YAML pipelines can access only repositories in their own project, for all projects in the organization.

Solution: In Organization settings > Pipelines > Settings, you enable Limit job authorization scope to current project for release pipelines.

Does this meet the goal?

options.text: Yes
No

explanation_html:
Correct answer: No.

The Limit job authorization scope to current project for release pipelines setting applies only to classic release pipelines. For YAML pipelines (and classic build pipelines), you must enable Limit job authorization scope to current project for non-release pipelines. Enabling it at the organization level restricts the scope to project for all projects, so the job token uses the project-scoped build identity ({Project} Build Service ({Org})) instead of the collection-scoped identity.

References:

  • Understand job access tokens

question_html:
Contoso enabled Protect access to repositories in YAML pipelines for a project. A YAML pipeline in the project builds the WebApp repository and runs a script that executes git clone to fetch the BuildTools repository from the same project by using System.AccessToken. Since the setting was enabled, the clone fails with an authorization error.

You need the pipeline to retrieve BuildTools while keeping the setting enabled. What should you do?

options.text: Declare BuildTools as a repository resource and add a checkout step for it in the job
Disable Limit job authorization scope to current project for non-release pipelines
Grant the Project Collection Build Service identity Read permission on BuildTools
Store a personal access token in a secret variable and use it in the git clone command

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Reference BuildTools explicitly with a checkout step (or a uses statement) in the job.

With Protect access to repositories in YAML pipelines enabled, the job access token is scoped to only the Azure DevOps repositories explicitly referenced by a checkout step or a uses statement in the job that uses that repository. Referencing the repository also triggers the protected-resource authorization for that repository.

Disabling the job authorization scope limit is incorrect because the repository is in the same project, so the scope isn't the cause; widening the scope also reduces security.

Granting Project Collection Build Service Read is incorrect because the token is still limited to explicitly referenced repositories, so an unreferenced clone continues to fail.

Using a personal access token is incorrect because it bypasses the control with a long-lived user credential, which defeats the purpose of the setting and adds secret-management risk.

References:

  • Understand job access tokens

question_html:
Tailspin Toys builds a public GitHub repository with Azure Pipelines. A project administrator sets Limit building pull requests from forked GitHub repositories to Securely build pull requests from forked repositories.

Which two statements describe how pipelines in the project behave for pull requests from forks? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: Pipelines can't make secrets available to builds of pull requests from forks
Builds of pull requests from forks must be triggered by a pull request comment
Builds of pull requests from forks run with the same permissions as regular builds
Builds of pull requests from forks run only on self-hosted agents
Pull requests from forks are never built by any pipeline in the project

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Secrets can't be made available to fork PR builds, and those builds must be triggered by a PR comment.

When Securely build pull requests from forked repositories is selected, all pipelines in scope cannot make secrets available to builds of PRs from forks, cannot make those builds have the same permissions as normal builds, and must be triggered by a PR comment. Projects can still choose not to build such PRs at all.

Same permissions as regular builds is incorrect because the secure option explicitly prevents enabling Make fork builds have the same permissions as regular builds.

Self-hosted agents only is incorrect because the setting doesn't select an agent pool; Microsoft actually recommends Microsoft-hosted agents for fork builds because they are discarded after each build.

Never built is incorrect because that is the separate Disable building pull requests from forked repositories option.

References:

  • Build GitHub repositories - Azure Pipelines
  • Secure agents, projects, and containers

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank runs self-hosted Windows build agents for Azure Pipelines. The agents currently run as a Microsoft Entra ID-backed service account that is a member of the Project Collection Service Accounts group. A security review flags this configuration as high risk.

You need to reduce the impact if a malicious pipeline runs on one of these agents. What should you do?

options.text: Reconfigure the agent service to run as a low-privileged local identity such as NT AUTHORITY\NETWORK SERVICE or a gMSA
Add the service account to the Project Collection Administrators group so that its permissions are audited centrally
Grant the agent pool Open access so that every pipeline in the project can use it
Share a single agent pool across all projects so that agents are monitored in one place

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Run the agent under a nonprivileged local account such as Network Service, Local Service, or a gMSA.

If an agent runs under an Entra ID-backed identity, a compromised pipeline can call Azure DevOps APIs directly with that identity rather than relying on the scoped job access token. Members of Project Collection Service Accounts are, by inheritance, also members of Project Collection Administrators, so a compromised pipeline could take over the organization. Microsoft recommends the lowest-privileged account possible.

Adding the account to Project Collection Administrators is incorrect because it increases privileges; the account is effectively already an administrator, which is the problem.

Granting Open access is incorrect because it lets every pipeline in the project use the pool, widening exposure instead of reducing it.

Sharing a single pool across projects is incorrect because Microsoft recommends separate pools per project to reduce lateral movement between projects.

References:

  • Secure agents, projects, and containers

question_html:
Litware's auditors found that users who can queue YAML pipelines in Azure DevOps add new variables in the Run pipeline panel, including variables that override system variables. You need to ensure that, for all projects in the organization, users can set only variables that the pipeline author explicitly allowed to be overridden at run time.

What should you enable in Organization settings > Pipelines > Settings?

options.text: Limit variables that can be set at queue time
Enable shell tasks arguments validation
Protect access to repositories in YAML pipelines
Limit job authorization scope to current project for non-release pipelines

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Limit variables that can be set at queue time.

When this setting is on, users can set at queue time only variables that are explicitly marked Settable at queue time (Classic) or Let users override this value when running this pipeline (YAML). The Add variable button disappears, and API calls that try to set other variables fail. Enabled at the organization level, it applies to all projects and can't be turned off per project.

Enable shell tasks arguments validation is incorrect because it validates the arguments input of built-in shell tasks against command injection; it doesn't restrict queue-time variables.

Protect access to repositories in YAML pipelines is incorrect because it limits which repositories the job token can access.

Limit job authorization scope is incorrect because it restricts the job access token to the current project; it doesn't control variables.

References:

  • Securely use variables and parameters

question_html:
Contoso has the following GitHub Actions workflow. The release job signs in to Azure by using OpenID Connect and then uses the GITHUB_TOKEN to create a GitHub release in the same repository. The repository's default workflow permissions are set to Read and write permissions.

on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']
permissions:
  id-token: write
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-sha>
      - uses: azure/login@<full-commit-sha>
        with:
          client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
      - run: gh release create "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" ./dist/*
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}

The repository is private. The checkout step fails, and the release can't be created. You need to fix the workflow by granting the least privileges required. What should you add to the permissions block?

options.text: contents: write
deployments: write
actions: write
Nothing; remove id-token: write so that the repository default permissions apply

explanation_html:
Correct answer: contents: write.

When you specify the access for any permission in a permissions block, all permissions that aren't specified are set to none, regardless of the repository default. Because only id-token: write is listed, the token has no contents access, so checkout (which needs read) and release creation (which needs write) both fail. contents: write covers both and keeps id-token: write for the OIDC sign-in to Azure.

deployments: write is incorrect because it covers deployment objects, not repository contents or releases.

actions: write is incorrect because it covers workflow runs and artifacts, not repository contents.

Removing id-token: write is incorrect because the Azure OIDC sign-in requires id-token: write, and falling back to read and write for all scopes isn't least privilege.

References:

  • Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions
  • Configuring OpenID Connect in Azure - GitHub Docs
  • Security hardening for GitHub Actions

question_html:
Fabrikam is replacing a client secret stored in GitHub with OpenID Connect for a workflow that deploys to Azure. A federated credential has been added to the Microsoft Entra app registration, and the repository has the secrets AZURE_CLIENT_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID, and AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID.

permissions:
  SLOT_1
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: azure/login@<full-commit-sha>
        with:
          client-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
          tenant-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ secrets.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}

What should you use for SLOT_1 so that the job can request an OIDC token?

options.text: id-token: write
id-token: read
deployments: write
secrets: read

explanation_html:
Correct answer: id-token: write.

To use OIDC with Azure, the workflow needs id-token: write so the job can request a JSON Web Token from the GitHub OIDC provider, and contents: read for repository access. The id-token: write permission only allows fetching the token; it doesn't grant write access to any repository or cloud resource.

id-token: read is incorrect because read access isn't enough to request an OIDC token; the documented value is write.

deployments: write is incorrect because it controls GitHub deployment objects and doesn't enable OIDC token requests.

secrets: read is incorrect because secrets isn't a GITHUB_TOKEN permission scope.

References:

  • Configuring OpenID Connect in Azure - GitHub Docs
  • Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions

question_html:
Adatum's workflow in the repository adatum/webshop runs on pushes to main. The deployment job is declared as follows:

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production

The repository was created in 2024 and hasn't opted in to immutable OIDC subject claims, so it uses the default subject claim format. The Microsoft Entra app registration has one federated credential with the subject repo:adatum/webshop:ref:refs/heads/main. The azure/login step fails because the token exchange is rejected. You need to add a federated credential that allows this job to sign in.

Which subject identifier should you use?

options.text: repo:adatum/webshop:environment:production
repo:adatum/webshop:ref:refs/heads/*
repo:adatum/webshop:pull-request
repo:adatum/webshop:environment:*

explanation_html:
Correct answer: repo:adatum/webshop:environment:production.

For jobs tied to a GitHub environment, the subject claim in the OIDC token has the format repo:<Organization/Repository>:environment:<Name>. The ref-based subject repo:...:ref:refs/heads/main is used only for jobs that aren't tied to an environment. The issuer and subject of the federated credential must exactly match the token claims, or the exchange fails.

The wildcard ref subject is incorrect because wildcard characters aren't supported in federated identity credential values, and the job is tied to an environment, so the subject isn't ref-based.

The pull-request subject is incorrect because it applies to workflows triggered by a pull request event, not to a push-triggered environment job.

The wildcard environment subject is incorrect because wildcards aren't supported; the subject must exactly match the environment name.

References:

  • Create a trust relationship between an app and an external identity provider
  • Configuring OpenID Connect in Azure - GitHub Docs

question_html:
Northwind uses GitHub Enterprise Cloud. A workflow deploys a web app by using a database password. You have the following requirements:

  • A member of the Operations team must approve every deployment to production.
  • Only runs from the main branch can deploy to production.
  • The database password must be available only to the production deployment job, and only after approval.

Which three actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Create a production environment and add the Operations team as required reviewers
Configure deployment branches and tags for the production environment to allow only main
Store the password as an environment secret in the production environment and reference the environment in the deployment job
Store the password as a repository secret and add an if: condition that checks github.ref
Configure a wait timer of 60 minutes on the production environment

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Required reviewers, deployment branch restrictions, and an environment secret.

Environment protection rules include required reviewers (up to six users or teams; one approval is enough) and deployment branches and tags (no restriction, protected branches only, or selected branches and tags). Environment secrets are available only to workflow jobs that reference the environment, and those jobs can access them only after configured protection rules, such as required reviewers, pass.

A repository secret with an if: condition is incorrect because repository secrets are available to any workflow job in the repository, and an expression in the workflow can be edited by anyone who can change the workflow; it doesn't require approval.

A wait timer is incorrect because it only delays the job for a period of time; it doesn't require approval or restrict branches.

References:

  • Managing environments for deployment
  • Deployments and environments - GitHub Docs

question_html:
Tailspin Toys uses a third-party action in its workflows, referenced as uses: vendor/scan-action@v3. After an industry incident in which an attacker moved a release tag to malicious code, the security team requires that every workflow run the exact, reviewed code of the action, even if the vendor's repository is compromised.

How should you reference the action?

options.text: uses: vendor/scan-action@<full-length 40-character commit SHA>
uses: vendor/scan-action@v3.4.1
uses: vendor/scan-action@main
uses: vendor/scan-action@<7-character short commit SHA>

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Pin the action to a full-length commit SHA.

GitHub recommends pinning actions to a full-length commit SHA; it is the way to use an action as an immutable release, because a bad actor would need to generate a SHA-1 collision for a valid Git object. Tags, including specific semantic version tags, can be moved or deleted by anyone who gains access to the action's repository. Organizations and repositories can also enforce this with the Require actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA policy.

A specific version tag is incorrect because a tag is mutable, which is exactly the attack described.

The main branch is incorrect because a branch reference changes with every commit, so the code isn't fixed at all.

A short SHA is incorrect because GitHub's guidance and the enforcement policy require the full-length SHA; a short SHA isn't accepted by the policy and is more prone to ambiguity.

References:

  • Security hardening for GitHub Actions
  • Managing GitHub Actions settings for a repository

question_html:
Wingtip Toys maintains a public GitHub repository. Integration tests require a secret API key. The tests are triggered by on: pull_request, and they fail for pull requests from forks because the secret is empty. You need the tests to run for fork pull requests without exposing the secret to untrusted code.

Solution: You change the trigger to on: pull_request_target and add a checkout step that checks out ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} before running the tests.

Does this meet the goal?

options.text: Yes
No

explanation_html:
Correct answer: No.

Except for GITHUB_TOKEN, secrets aren't passed to the runner when a workflow is triggered from a forked repository, which is why the key is empty. Workflows triggered by pull_request_target run in the privileged context of the base repository and can have write access and access to referenced secrets. Combining this trigger with a checkout of the untrusted pull request code runs attacker-controlled code with access to the secret, which is the exact risk GitHub warns about.

References:

  • Using secrets in GitHub Actions
  • Security hardening for GitHub Actions

question_html:
Contoso develops a commercial, closed-source web application that is offered only as a hosted SaaS service; Contoso never distributes binaries to customers. The legal team requires the build pipeline to fail if a dependency's license would require Contoso to publish its source code because users interact with the software over a network.

Which license should be added to the denied list in the software composition analysis policy to meet this specific requirement?

options.text: AGPL-3.0
GPL-3.0
LGPL-2.1
Apache-2.0

explanation_html:
Correct answer: AGPL-3.0.

The AGPL is a strong copyleft license whose obligations are triggered when software is made available over a network, so it is unacceptable for a proprietary SaaS offering. GPL v2 and v3 obligations are triggered by distribution of binaries, not by SaaS use, so they don't trigger source disclosure for a hosted service that's never distributed. SCA tools in the pipeline can enforce such license policies, for example by failing the build on denied licenses.

GPL-3.0 is incorrect because its source-disclosure obligation is triggered by distributing binaries; the GPL doesn't require source disclosure for SaaS offerings.

LGPL-2.1 is incorrect because it is a weak copyleft license that generally allows use in proprietary applications, and it isn't triggered by network use.

Apache-2.0 is incorrect because it is a permissive license whose main obligation is attribution.

References:

  • Examine license implications and ratings
  • Integrate software composition analysis checks into pipelines

question_html:
Litware wants to connect its Azure DevOps organization to Microsoft Defender for Cloud so that the security team can see DevOps inventory and DevOps environment posture recommendations.
