A security engineer will create the connector from Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > Add environment > Azure DevOps.

Which three prerequisites must be met? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: The engineer has the Contributor role on the Azure subscription where the connector is created
The engineer is a Project Collection Administrator in the Azure DevOps organization
Third-party application access via OAuth is set to On for the Azure DevOps organization
The Microsoft Security DevOps extension is installed and running in every pipeline
The engineer has the Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Contributor on the subscription, Project Collection Administrator on the organization, and Third-party application access via OAuth enabled.

To create the Azure DevOps connector, you need Contributor on the Azure subscription (Security Admin is also listed as sufficient), Project Collection Administrator on the organization with Basic access level (Stakeholder isn't sufficient), and the organization policy Third-party application access via OAuth set to On. After onboarding, resources can take up to 8 hours to appear.

The Microsoft Security DevOps extension is incorrect because it isn't required to connect the organization or to see inventory and environment posture recommendations; it is an optional prerequisite for some scanning findings and code-to-cloud mapping.

Global Administrator is incorrect because no Microsoft Entra directory role is required; the documented permissions are at the subscription and Azure DevOps organization levels.

References:

  • Connect your Azure DevOps organizations to Defender for Cloud
  • DevOps security support and prerequisites

question_html:
Fabrikam connected its Azure DevOps organization to Microsoft Defender for Cloud and currently uses only the free Foundational CSPM capabilities. Developers want Defender for Cloud to add pull request annotations in Azure Repos for Infrastructure as Code findings, and the security team wants code-to-cloud mapping for container images built by the pipelines.

What should you do first?

options.text: Enable the Defender Cloud Security Posture Management (Defender CSPM) plan
Enable the Defender for Servers Plan 2
Enable the Defender for App Service plan
Create a second Azure DevOps connector for the same organization in another subscription

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Enable the Defender CSPM plan.

Foundational CSPM includes the DevOps inventory and security recommendations (for example, DevOps environment misconfigurations and, with the right scanners, code, secrets and dependency findings). Pull request annotations, code-to-cloud mapping for containers and IaC, attack path analysis, and cloud security explorer require the paid Defender CSPM plan.

Defender for Servers Plan 2 is incorrect because it protects servers and VMs; it doesn't enable DevOps PR annotations or code-to-cloud mapping.

Defender for App Service is incorrect because it provides threat protection for App Service apps, not DevOps posture capabilities.

A second connector is incorrect because only one instance of an Azure DevOps organization can be onboarded to a tenant, and a second connector wouldn't add paid-plan features.

References:

  • DevOps security support and prerequisites
  • Microsoft Defender for Cloud DevOps security benefits

question_html:
Contoso has a monorepo. A GitHub Actions workflow must run for pull requests that target main only when files under src/ change. Changes that touch only files under src/docs/ must not trigger the workflow.

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - 'src/**'
      SLOT_1

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: - '!src/docs/**'
paths-ignore: ['src/docs/**']
- 'src/docs/**'
- '^src/docs/**'

explanation_html:
Correct answer: - '!src/docs/**'

Within a paths filter, a pattern prefixed with ! that matches after a positive pattern excludes the path. Because 'src/**' comes first and '!src/docs/**' comes after it, a change limited to src/docs/ no longer triggers the workflow, while other changes under src/ still do.

paths-ignore is incorrect because you cannot use both paths and paths-ignore for the same event. When you need to include and exclude paths together, you use paths with ! patterns.

- 'src/docs/**' is incorrect because a positive pattern adds the docs folder as another trigger path. It does not exclude it.

- '^src/docs/**' is incorrect because ^ is not the negation character in GitHub Actions filter patterns. Only ! negates a pattern.

References:

  • Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions

question_html:
Tailspin Toys maintains a public open source repository on GitHub. Many pull requests come from forks. The maintainers want a workflow that automatically adds labels and a welcome comment to every new pull request, including pull requests from forks. The workflow needs a token that can write to the base repository. It never builds or runs code from the pull request.

Which workflow trigger should you use?

options.text: pull_request_target
pull_request
push
workflow_dispatch

explanation_html:
Correct answer: pull_request_target

pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository's default branch, not the merge commit of the pull request. Because of that, it has access to secrets and a token that can write to the base repository, even when the pull request comes from a fork. That is what labeling and commenting workflows need. GitHub warns against using this event to build or run code from the pull request, and this scenario does neither.

pull_request is incorrect because when it is triggered from a fork, secrets are not passed to the runner and GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only. The workflow could not add labels or comments.

push is incorrect because opening a pull request from a fork does not push to the base repository, so the workflow would never run for these pull requests.

workflow_dispatch is incorrect because it only starts runs manually or through the API. It does not react automatically to new pull requests.

References:

  • Events that trigger workflows

question_html:
Fabrikam has two workflows in the same repository. The workflow named CI builds and tests the code. A second workflow must deploy to the staging environment only after a CI run on main has finished successfully.

name: Deploy staging
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: ["CI"]
    types: [SLOT_1]
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  deploy:
    if: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying"

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: completed
success
requested
closed

explanation_html:
Correct answer: completed

The workflow_run event supports the activity types completed, requested and in_progress. completed fires when the CI run finishes, whatever its result. The job-level if then checks github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' so that the deployment runs only after a successful run. Note that workflow_run triggers only if the workflow file exists on the default branch.

success is incorrect because it is not an activity type of workflow_run. Success is a conclusion, which you check in the if condition.

requested is incorrect because it fires when the CI run is requested, before it has built or tested anything.

closed is incorrect because it is an activity type for pull requests and issues, not for workflow_run.

References:

  • Events that trigger workflows

question_html:
Northwind Traders' default branch is main. A developer wants a nightly regression suite to run against the latest code on a long-lived branch named release/2.0. main must not be tested by this workflow.

Solution: On the release/2.0 branch only, the developer adds a workflow file with on: schedule: - cron: '0 2 * * *'.

Does this meet the goal?

options.text: Yes
No

explanation_html:
Correct answer: No

Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. A schedule trigger in a workflow file that exists only on release/2.0 never fires. To test the release branch, put the scheduled workflow on main and have it check out release/2.0 explicitly. For example, set ref: release/2.0 on actions/checkout.

References:

  • Events that trigger workflows

question_html:
Litware wants operators to start a deployment workflow manually from the Actions tab. The operator must pick the target from a drop-down list with exactly the values dev, test and prod. These values are not configured as GitHub environments.

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      target:
        description: 'Deployment target'
        required: true
        type: SLOT_1
        options:
          - dev
          - test
          - prod

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: choice
string
environment
enum

explanation_html:
Correct answer: choice

A workflow_dispatch input of type choice shows a drop-down list built from its options list. The workflow file must be on the default branch for the Run workflow button to appear.

string is incorrect because it shows a free-text box and ignores options, so operators could enter any value.

environment is incorrect because it fills the drop-down list from the repository's configured GitHub environments, not from an options list. The values here are not environments.

enum is incorrect because it is not a supported input type for workflow_dispatch.

References:

  • Events that trigger workflows

question_html:
Adatum requires the status check build on main through a branch protection rule. The build job is in a workflow that is triggered by pull_request with a paths: ['src/**'] filter. Pull requests that change only README.md stay blocked with the message "Waiting for status to be reported".

You need documentation-only pull requests to be mergeable. The build check must stay required for code changes. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the paths filter so that the workflow runs for every pull request, and use a job-level if condition that skips the build job when no files under src/ changed.
Replace the paths filter with paths-ignore: ['README.md'].
Clear the "Require branches to be up to date before merging" setting on the branch protection rule.
Add if: always() to the build job.

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Remove the paths filter and skip the job with a job-level if condition instead.

When a workflow is skipped because of path filtering, branch filtering or a commit message, its checks stay Pending, and a pull request that requires them cannot be merged. A job that is skipped by a conditional, however, reports Success. So the workflow should always start, and the job should decide whether to do real work. For example, it can use an earlier job that detects which files changed.

paths-ignore is incorrect because it is still path filtering. Documentation-only pull requests would still skip the whole workflow and leave the required check pending.

Clearing "Require branches to be up to date" is incorrect because that setting only switches between strict and loose status checks. The required check would still never be reported.

if: always() is incorrect because the workflow never starts when its path filter does not match, so job-level conditions are never evaluated.

References:

  • Troubleshooting required status checks
  • Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions

question_html:
Wingtip Toys has the following workflow. The notify job must post a message to the team chat only if build or test fails.

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./build.sh
  test:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./test.sh
  notify:
    needs: [build, test]
    if: SLOT_1
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./notify.sh

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: ${{ failure() }}
${{ always() }}
${{ needs.test.result == 'failure' }}
${{ cancelled() }}

explanation_html:
Correct answer: ${{ failure() }}

In a job with dependencies, failure() returns true if any ancestor job failed. Because it is a status check function, it also replaces the implicit success() check, so notify runs even though a job it needs did not succeed.

always() is incorrect because notify would also run after successful builds.

needs.test.result == 'failure' is incorrect because the expression has no status check function, so success() is still applied implicitly. After any failure, the condition is false and notify is skipped. Also, if build fails, test is skipped rather than failed.

cancelled() is incorrect because it is true only when the workflow run was cancelled, not when a job fails.

References:

  • Evaluate expressions in workflows and actions
  • Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions

question_html:
Contoso uses the following matrix strategy:

strategy:
  matrix:
    os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
    node: [18, 20]
    exclude:
      - os: windows-latest
        node: 18
    include:
      - os: ubuntu-latest
        node: 22
      - os: windows-latest
        node: 18

How many jobs does the matrix create?
explanation_html:
Correct answer: 5

The base matrix has 2 × 2 = 4 combinations. exclude removes windows-latest/18, which leaves 3. All include combinations are processed after exclude. An include entry is merged into existing combinations only if it does not overwrite any original matrix value. Otherwise it is added as a new combination.

  • ubuntu-latest/22 would overwrite node in every existing combination, so it becomes a new job (4).
  • windows-latest/18 cannot merge without overwriting either os or node, so it is added back as a new job, even though it was excluded earlier (5).

3 is incorrect because it ignores both include entries.

4 is incorrect because it assumes that the excluded combination cannot be added back. include is processed after exclude, so it can be.

6 is incorrect because it assumes that exclude is applied after include, or that it is ignored.

References:

  • Running variations of jobs in a workflow

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank runs a long CI workflow on pull_request events. When a developer pushes a new commit to a pull request, any CI run still in progress for that same pull request must be cancelled. Runs for other pull requests must not be affected.

Solution: You add the following to the workflow:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.run_id }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

Does this meet the goal?

options.text: Yes
No

explanation_html:
Correct answer: No

cancel-in-progress cancels only runs that are in the same concurrency group. github.run_id is unique for every run, so each run gets its own group and nothing is ever cancelled. Use a key that stays the same across pushes to one pull request, such as group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.head_ref || github.run_id }}. The github.run_id fallback only matters for events where head_ref is undefined.

References:

  • Control the concurrency of workflows and jobs

question_html:
Fabrikam's platform team publishes a reusable workflow at .github/workflows/deploy-webapp.yml in the repository fabrikam/platform-workflows. The workflow declares on: workflow_call with an input named app-name and a secret named deploy-key. An application team must call version v2 of it.

jobs:
  deploy-prod:
    SLOT_1: fabrikam/platform-workflows/.github/workflows/deploy-webapp.yml@v2
    with:
      app-name: fabrikam-web
    secrets:
      deploy-key: ${{ secrets.PROD_DEPLOY_KEY }}

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: uses
run
workflow
call

explanation_html:
Correct answer: uses

A reusable workflow is called directly at the job level with jobs.<job_id>.uses, in the form {owner}/{repo}/.github/workflows/{filename}@{ref}. The ref can be a SHA, a release tag or a branch. Inputs are passed with with, and secrets are passed with secrets.

run is incorrect because run executes shell commands inside a step. It is not a job-level keyword.

workflow and call are incorrect because neither is a job-level keyword in GitHub Actions workflow syntax.

References:

  • Reusing workflows
  • Reusable workflows reference

question_html:
Northwind Traders calls a reusable workflow from the following job:

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    uses: northwind/shared/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@v1
    with:
      region: westeurope

The workflow fails validation. Deployments must still go through the production environment's protection rules.

What should you do?

options.text: Remove runs-on and environment from the calling job. In the reusable workflow, add an input for the environment name and set environment on the job that deploys.
Move the uses line into a steps list under the deploy job, and keep runs-on and environment.
Replace environment: production with secrets: inherit.
Convert deploy.yml to a composite action and set environment: production in the action metadata.

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Remove runs-on and environment from the calling job, and set the environment inside the reusable workflow, passing its name as an input.

Only these keywords are supported in a job that calls a reusable workflow: name, uses, with, secrets (including secrets: inherit), strategy, needs, if, concurrency, permissions and cache-mode. runs-on and environment belong on the jobs inside the called workflow, where the environment's protection rules are enforced.

Moving uses into steps is incorrect because a reusable workflow cannot be called from a step. A step-level uses references an action, not a workflow file.

secrets: inherit is incorrect because it only passes secrets. It does not attach the job to an environment or apply its protection rules, and runs-on would still be invalid.

Converting to a composite action is incorrect because composite actions contain steps only and cannot declare jobs or environments.

References:

  • Reusable workflows reference
  • Reusing workflows

question_html:
Contoso's repositories are all in the same GitHub organization. A caller workflow invokes an organization-wide reusable workflow that reads about a dozen repository and organization secrets. The team wants to stop listing every secret by name in the caller.

jobs:
  release:
    uses: contoso/.github-workflows/.github/workflows/release.yml@main
    secrets: SLOT_1

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: inherit
all
${{ secrets }}
${{ toJSON(secrets) }}

explanation_html:
Correct answer: inherit

secrets: inherit passes the caller's secrets to the called workflow implicitly. It works when both workflows are in the same organization or enterprise. Secrets pass only to the directly called workflow. In a deeper chain, each intermediate workflow must pass them on explicitly.

all is incorrect because it is not a valid value for secrets. The only keyword is inherit. Otherwise you provide a mapping of named secrets.

${{ secrets }} and ${{ toJSON(secrets) }} are incorrect because secrets on a calling job expects either inherit or a map of individual secret names. A whole context object or a JSON string is not accepted as the secret set.

References:

  • Reusing workflows

question_html:
Litware's DevOps team is deciding between composite actions and reusable workflows to standardize CI across 40 repositories.

Which two statements are true? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: A composite action runs as steps inside the calling job on the caller's runner, and the log shows it as a single step.
A reusable workflow can contain multiple jobs, and each job can specify its own runner.
A composite action can define jobs that target a GitHub environment with required reviewers.
A reusable workflow is referenced from a step in the caller's steps list, the same way as an action.
Environment variables that the caller sets in a workflow-level env block are automatically available in a called reusable workflow.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: The composite action statement and the reusable workflow multiple-jobs statement.

A composite action bundles steps that run within the caller's job, on the caller's machine, and it appears in the log as one step. A reusable workflow can contain several jobs, and each job can choose its own runner and environment.

Composite action with jobs and environments is incorrect because composite actions contain only steps. They cannot define jobs or target environments.

Reusable workflow referenced from a step is incorrect because a reusable workflow is called directly within a job (jobs.<id>.uses), not from a step.

Workflow-level env propagating is incorrect because environment variables set in the caller's workflow-level env context are not propagated to the called workflow. Pass values as inputs instead.

References:

  • Avoiding duplication (reusable workflows vs composite actions)
  • Reusable workflows reference
  • Creating a composite action

question_html:
Adatum calls a reusable workflow from ci.yml. The called workflow must use the value of DOTNET_VERSION that the caller sets.

Solution: In ci.yml, you add env: DOTNET_VERSION: '8.0.x' at the workflow level. In the reusable workflow, you reference ${{ env.DOTNET_VERSION }}.

Does this meet the goal?

options.text: Yes
No

explanation_html:
Correct answer: No

Environment variables set in a workflow-level env context in the caller workflow are not propagated to the called workflow. Instead, declare an input under on.workflow_call.inputs in the reusable workflow, pass it with with: dotnet-version: '8.0.x' in the calling job, and read it with ${{ inputs.dotnet-version }}.

References:

  • Reusable workflows reference

question_html:
Tailspin Toys has a reusable workflow that builds and pushes a container image. Callers need the image tag as a workflow output.

on:
  workflow_call:
    outputs:
      image-tag:
        description: "Tag of the pushed image"
        value: SLOT_1
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      tag: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tag }}
    steps:
      - id: meta
        run: echo "tag=1.0.${{ github.run_number }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: ${{ jobs.build.outputs.tag }}
${{ steps.meta.outputs.tag }}
${{ needs.build.outputs.tag }}
${{ env.tag }}

explanation_html:
Correct answer: ${{ jobs.build.outputs.tag }}

Outputs flow in three steps: a step writes to GITHUB_OUTPUT, the job maps it into jobs.build.outputs, and on.workflow_call.outputs.<name>.value references the job output through the jobs context.

steps.meta.outputs.tag is incorrect because step outputs are visible only inside their own job. A workflow-level output must reference a job output.

needs.build.outputs.tag is incorrect because the needs context is used by a dependent job inside a workflow, not in the workflow_call outputs definition.

env.tag is incorrect because no environment variable named tag is set, and outputs are not exposed through env.

References:

  • Reusing workflows
  • Passing information between jobs

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank calculates a version number in one job and uses it in a later job.

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.ver.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - id: ver
        run: echo "version=2.3.${{ github.run_number }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying ${{ SLOT_1 }}"

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: needs.build.outputs.version
jobs.build.outputs.version
steps.ver.outputs.version
env.version

explanation_html:
Correct answer: needs.build.outputs.version

A dependent job reads an upstream job's outputs with needs.<job_id>.outputs.<output_name>. The needs: build dependency is required for that context to be available.

jobs.build.outputs.version is incorrect because the jobs context is available only in a reusable workflow's on.workflow_call.outputs, not inside a job's steps.

steps.ver.outputs.version is incorrect because the ver step belongs to the build job. The steps context only covers steps in the current job.

env.version is incorrect because writing to GITHUB_OUTPUT creates a step output, not an environment variable. Even GITHUB_ENV only affects later steps in the same job.

References:

  • Passing information between jobs

question_html:
Wingtip Toys builds firmware. The integration tests must flash the firmware onto a physical test device that is connected by USB to a workstation in the company lab. The device-flashing toolchain has a node-locked license that is installed on that workstation.

Which type of runner should run the integration test job?

options.text: A self-hosted runner installed on the lab workstation
A standard GitHub-hosted runner (ubuntu-latest) that installs the toolchain at the start of the job
A GitHub-hosted larger runner with Azure private networking
A GitHub-hosted larger runner with a static IP address

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A self-hosted runner installed on the lab workstation.

Self-hosted runners run on machines you manage, so a job can use locally attached hardware and software that is licensed to that machine. You can give the runner a custom label, such as firmware-lab, and target it with runs-on: [self-hosted, firmware-lab].

Standard GitHub-hosted runner is incorrect because every job gets a new GitHub-hosted VM. It cannot reach a USB device in your lab, and a node-locked license cannot move to it.

Larger runner with Azure private networking is incorrect because private networking gives network access to resources in an Azure virtual network. It does not give physical access to a USB device in the lab.

Larger runner with a static IP address is incorrect because a static IP only helps with firewall allowlisting. It does not solve the hardware or licensing requirement.

References:

  • About GitHub-hosted runners
  • Using self-hosted runners in a workflow

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank's workflows upload packages to a partner's SaaS endpoint. The partner's firewall only accepts traffic from IP addresses on an allowlist. Woodgrove wants GitHub to manage the runner infrastructure. The bank does not want to patch or scale any runner VMs itself.

What should you use?

options.text: GitHub-hosted larger runners with static IP addresses
Standard GitHub-hosted runners, adding the IP ranges from the GitHub meta API to the allowlist once
Self-hosted runners on Azure virtual machines with public IP addresses
A GitHub environment with a deployment branch policy

explanation_html:
Correct answer: GitHub-hosted larger runners with static IP addresses.

Larger runners are managed by GitHub and can be assigned static IP addresses from a specific range. A partner can then allowlist that range in its firewall. Larger runners are billed per minute and do not use the included minutes.

Standard GitHub-hosted runners with the meta API ranges is incorrect because standard runners don't have dedicated static IPs. The published ranges are very large, shared and change over time, so a one-time allowlist is neither safe nor reliable.

Self-hosted runners on Azure VMs is incorrect because they would meet the IP requirement, but Woodgrove would have to manage, patch and scale the VMs itself.

Environment with a deployment branch policy is incorrect because environment rules control which branches can deploy. They have no effect on the source IP address of the runner.

References:

  • About larger runners

question_html:
Contoso's GitHub organization uses the GitHub Team plan. Contoso registers four self-hosted runners at the organization level on servers that can reach the finance database. Only the three finance repositories may run jobs on these runners.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Create a runner group in the organization settings and set its repository access to the three finance repositories only.
Move the four finance runners into the new runner group, or register them with the --runnergroup option.
Add a custom label named finance to the runners and tell finance teams to use runs-on: [self-hosted, finance].
Add the finance runners to a CODEOWNERS entry for .github/workflows/.
Create a GitHub environment named finance with required reviewers.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Create a runner group with repository access limited to the finance repositories, and place the runners in that group.

Runner groups control which repositories can use a set of organization-level self-hosted runners. On the Team plan and higher, you can create extra groups and set repository access to Selected repositories. New runners go into the default group unless you register them with --runnergroup. You can also move existing runners between groups.

Custom label is incorrect because labels only route jobs. Any repository with access to the runners could still target the finance label.

CODEOWNERS is incorrect because it only requests reviews for file changes. It cannot restrict runner access, and runners are not code owners.

Environment with required reviewers is incorrect because it adds approvals to jobs that reference the environment. It does not stop other repositories from using the runners.

References:

  • Managing access to self-hosted runners using groups

question_html:
Fabrikam's .NET workflow restores NuGet packages. The cache must be reused until a packages.lock.json file changes. When a lock file changes, the workflow should fall back to the most recent NuGet cache for the same OS.

- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.nuget/packages
    key: ${{ runner.os }}-nuget-${{ SLOT_1 }}
    restore-keys: |
      ${{ runner.os }}-nuget-

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: hashFiles('**/packages.lock.json')
github.sha
github.run_id
format('**/packages.lock.json')

explanation_html:
Correct answer: hashFiles('**/packages.lock.json')

hashFiles returns a SHA-256 hash of the matched files. The key stays the same while the lock files are unchanged, which gives an exact hit (cache-hit is true). When a lock file changes, the key changes. The restore-keys prefix then matches the most recently created cache that starts with <os>-nuget-, and a new cache is saved under the new key.

github.sha is incorrect because the key would change on every commit, so an exact hit would almost never happen, and a new cache would be saved each time.

github.run_id is incorrect because it is unique for every run, so an exact match never happens.

format('**/packages.lock.json') is incorrect because format only interpolates strings. It returns the constant pattern text, so the key never changes when dependencies change.

References:

  • Caching dependencies to speed up workflows
  • Evaluate expressions in workflows and actions

question_html:
Northwind Traders' default branch is main. A developer opens pull request #42 from feature/payments into main. The following caches exist:

  • A cache created by a push workflow run on main
  • A cache created by an earlier workflow run for pull request #42
  • A cache created by a push run on the sibling branch feature/invoices
  • A cache created by a workflow run for pull request #40

A new pull_request workflow run starts for pull request #42. Which two caches can it restore? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

options.text: The cache created on main
The cache created by the earlier run for pull request #42
The cache created on feature/invoices
The cache created for pull request #40

explanation_html:
Correct answers: The cache created on main, and the cache from the earlier run of pull request #42.

A workflow run can restore caches created in the current branch, in the default branch, and, for pull requests, in the base branch. Caches from a pull_request run are scoped to the pull request's merge ref, so later runs of the same pull request can use them.

feature/invoices is incorrect because a run cannot restore caches from sibling branches.

Pull request #40 is incorrect because pull request caches are scoped to that pull request's merge ref, and other pull requests cannot access them.

References:

  • Caching dependencies to speed up workflows

question_html:
Adatum's Node.js workflow uses actions/setup-node and then runs npm ci. You need to cache the npm dependencies between runs with the least amount of workflow configuration.

What should you do?

options.text: Set the cache input of actions/setup-node to npm.
Add an actions/cache step that caches node_modules with key ${{ github.sha }}.
Upload node_modules with actions/upload-artifact at the end of each run and download it at the start of the next run.
Add a concurrency group so that only one workflow run installs dependencies at a time.

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Set cache: npm on actions/setup-node.

The setup-* actions, including setup-node, setup-python and setup-java, have built-in dependency caching that needs minimal configuration. They create and restore the cache with a key based on the lock file.

actions/cache with ${{ github.sha }} is incorrect because it takes more configuration, and a commit-based key creates a new cache on every commit, so exact hits are rare.

Artifacts is incorrect because artifacts are meant for keeping files that a workflow produces, such as build outputs and logs. They are not meant for reusing dependencies across runs, and downloading an artifact from another run takes a run ID and a token.

Concurrency group is incorrect because it limits parallel runs. It does not cache anything.

References:

  • Caching dependencies to speed up workflows

question_html:
Litware uploads test result files in every CI run. To reduce storage usage, these artifacts must be deleted automatically after five days. Other artifacts in the repository must keep the default retention period.

- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  with:
    name: test-results
    path: TestResults/
    SLOT_1: 5

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: retention-days
expire-days
retention
if-no-files-found

explanation_html:
Correct answer: retention-days

By default, artifacts are kept for 90 days. The retention-days input of actions/upload-artifact overrides this for one artifact. The value cannot exceed the limit set for the repository, organization or enterprise. Changing the repository-level setting would also affect other artifacts.

expire-days and retention are incorrect because neither is an input of actions/upload-artifact.

if-no-files-found is incorrect because it is a real input, but it controls what happens when the path matches no files (warn, error or ignore). It does not set retention.

References:

  • Storing and sharing data from a workflow

question_html:
Contoso deploys to Azure from a job that references the GitHub environment production. Requirements:

  • A member of the release-managers team must approve each production deployment before the job starts.
  • Only workflow runs from the main branch can deploy to production.

Which two settings should you configure? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: On the production environment, add the release-managers team as required reviewers.
On the production environment, set deployment branches and tags to Selected branches and tags and add a rule for main.
Add a branch protection rule on main that requires one approving review before merging.
Add a CODEOWNERS entry that assigns .github/workflows/ to the release-managers team.
On the production environment, set a wait timer of 0 minutes.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Required reviewers on the environment, and a deployment branch rule that allows only main.

Environment protection rules apply to every job that references the environment. Required reviewers (up to six people or teams) pause the job until one of them approves. A Selected branches and tags deployment policy limits which refs can deploy to the environment. Environment secrets become available only after the rules pass.

Branch protection requiring a review is incorrect because it controls merging into main, not approval of each deployment. It also doesn't stop other branches from deploying.

CODEOWNERS is incorrect because it requests reviews on pull requests that change workflow files. It doesn't gate deployment runs.

Wait timer of 0 minutes is incorrect because a wait timer only delays a job. A value of 0 adds no control.

References:

  • Managing environments for deployment

question_html:
Tailspin Toys deploys an ASP.NET Core app to Azure App Service. The workflow must deploy to the existing staging deployment slot so the team can swap it into production later.

- uses: azure/login@v2
  with:
    client-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
    tenant-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
    subscription-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
- uses: azure/webapps-deploy@v3
  with:
    app-name: tailspin-web
    package: ./publish
    SLOT_1: staging

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: slot-name
deployment-slot
target-path
environment

explanation_html:
Correct answer: slot-name

azure/webapps-deploy@v3 takes the app name in app-name, the folder or package in package, and an existing non-production slot in slot-name. If slot-name is not set, it deploys to production. Authentication comes from the preceding azure/login step, which uses OpenID Connect with the client, tenant and subscription IDs.

deployment-slot is incorrect because it is not an input of the action.

target-path is incorrect because it is a real input, but it sets the folder inside the web app (for example /home/site/wwwroot), not the slot.

environment is incorrect because it is not an input of azure/webapps-deploy. It is a job-level key for GitHub environments, and on azure/login it selects the Azure cloud.

References:

  • Deploy to App Service by using GitHub Actions
  • azure/webapps-deploy v3 action.yml

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank's repository core-banking has the following rules that target main:

  • An active organization ruleset that requires a pull request with 1 approving review
  • An active repository ruleset that requires a pull request with 2 approving reviews
  • A classic branch protection rule that requires 1 approving review

How many approving reviews does a pull request into main need before it can be merged?

options.text: 1, because the organization ruleset overrides repository-level rules
2, because the rules are aggregated and the most restrictive version applies
4, because the review requirements of all rules are added together
1, because the branch protection rule takes precedence over rulesets

explanation_html:
Correct answer: 2

Unlike branch protection rules, several rulesets can apply to the same branch at once. When more than one ruleset, or a ruleset and a branch protection rule, target the same branch, the rules are aggregated. If the same rule is set differently, the most restrictive version applies, so 2 approving reviews are required.

Organization ruleset overrides is incorrect because rule layers do not override each other by level. They are combined.

Requirements added together is incorrect because aggregation applies the strictest value. It does not add the counts.

Branch protection takes precedence is incorrect because rulesets and branch protection rules are layered and both apply.

References:

  • About rulesets

question_html:
Fabrikam's .github/CODEOWNERS file on main contains:

*          @fabrikam/developers
/infra/    @fabrikam/platform
*.md       @fabrikam/docs

The branch protection rule for main has Require review from Code Owners enabled. A pull request into main changes only infra/README.md.

Whose approval satisfies the code owner review requirement?

options.text: A member of @fabrikam/docs
A member of @fabrikam/platform
A member of @fabrikam/developers
One member from each of the three teams

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A member of @fabrikam/docs

In a CODEOWNERS file, order matters, and the last matching pattern takes precedence. infra/README.md matches all three lines, but *.md is the last match, so only the docs team owns the file. The file must be on the base branch (main) for review requests to be sent.

@fabrikam/platform is incorrect because the /infra/ pattern is overridden by the later *.md match.

@fabrikam/developers is incorrect because * is the first match and is overridden by both later patterns.

One member from each team is incorrect because only the last matching pattern decides ownership. Owners from different lines are not combined.

References:

  • About code owners

question_html:
Contoso's GitHub repository is connected to an Azure Boards project that uses the Agile process. A pull request into the default branch main has the title Payment fixes AB#104 and this description:

Fixes AB#101, AB#102 and fixes AB#103

The pull request is merged. Which two work items are moved to the first state in the Resolved category? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
explanation_html:
Correct answers: 101 and 103

Azure Boards applies a fix/fixes/fixed keyword only to the AB# reference directly after it. In a list such as Fixes AB#123, AB#124, every item is linked, but only the first one changes state. Here Fixes applies to 101 and the second fixes applies to 103. Items are moved to the first state in the Resolved category, or to the Completed category if the process has no Resolved state. State transitions happen only when the pull request is merged into the default branch.

102 is incorrect because it is linked, but no transition keyword comes directly before it.

104 is incorrect because an AB# mention in a pull request title doesn't create a link, so the work item isn't linked or changed.

References:

  • Link GitHub commits, PRs, branches, and issues to work items

question_html:
Litware connected its Azure Boards project to several GitHub.com repositories with a fine-grained personal access token. Developers now want Azure Boards pull request status checks to appear on their GitHub pull requests. They also want to use the GitHub Copilot integration with Azure Boards.

What should you do?

options.text: Replace the PAT connection with a connection that authenticates with a GitHub.com user account, so that the Azure Boards app for GitHub is installed.
Regenerate the fine-grained PAT with the Checks permission set to Read and write, and update the connection.
Replace the fine-grained PAT with a classic PAT that has the repo, read:user, user:email and admin:repo_hook scopes.
Register Azure DevOps as an OAuth app in GitHub and add an OAuth configuration in the organization settings.

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Recreate the connection with a GitHub.com user account so that the Azure Boards app for GitHub is used.

PAT connections, including fine-grained PATs, do not support pull request status checks or the GitHub Copilot integration. Both features need a GitHub App connection, which you get by connecting with a GitHub.com user account. That is the recommended option for GitHub.com.

Adding a Checks permission to the PAT is incorrect because the limitation applies to PAT connections in general, whatever permissions the token has.

Classic PAT is incorrect because those scopes are what a classic PAT connection needs, but it is still a PAT connection and has the same limitations.

OAuth app registration is incorrect because OAuth configurations are used to connect to GitHub Enterprise Server, not GitHub.com.

References:

  • Connect an Azure Boards project to a GitHub repository

question_html:
Contoso has an ASP.NET Core web app that reads settings from Azure App Configuration. Default values for every key are stored with no label. A subset of keys has an environment-specific value stored with the label Production.

When the app runs in production, it must use the Production value for a key when one exists and fall back to the unlabeled value for every other key.

builder.Configuration.AddAzureAppConfiguration(options =>
{
    options.Connect(new Uri(endpoint), new DefaultAzureCredential())
           SLOT_1;
});

What should you use for SLOT_1? (env contains builder.Environment.EnvironmentName.)

options.text:
.Select(KeyFilter.Any, LabelFilter.Null)
.Select(KeyFilter.Any, env)

.Select(KeyFilter.Any, env)
.Select(KeyFilter.Any, LabelFilter.Null)
.Select(KeyFilter.Any, env)
.Select("Production:*", LabelFilter.Null)

explanation_html:
Correct answer: .Select(KeyFilter.Any, LabelFilter.Null).Select(KeyFilter.Any, env)

App Configuration providers stack selectors: key-values loaded by a later Select call overwrite matching keys loaded by an earlier one, so the last loaded value wins. Loading the unlabeled defaults first and then the environment label means a Production value overrides the default when it exists, and every other key keeps its unlabeled value.

Reversed order is incorrect because the unlabeled values are loaded last and overwrite the Production values, so the overrides never take effect.

Selecting only the environment label is incorrect because keys that have no Production value are not loaded at all. By default the provider loads only unlabeled key-values, and once you call Select you get only what you select, so there is no fallback.

Selecting keys with a Production: prefix is incorrect because a key prefix is part of the key name. Production:Timeout and Timeout are different keys, so nothing is overridden. Labels, not prefixes, are the App Configuration feature for per-environment variations of the same key.

References:

  • Use labels to provide per-environment configuration values
  • Azure App Configuration best practices

question_html:
Fabrikam's operations team changes about 20 related key-values in Azure App Configuration as one batch, for example when switching to a new payment provider. The ASP.NET Core app uses dynamic configuration refresh.

Running instances must reload configuration only once, after the whole batch is written. They must never run with a mix of old and new values from a half-finished update.

How should you configure refresh in the App Configuration provider?

options.text: Call refreshOptions.Register("Payments:Sentinel", refreshAll: true) and update the Payments:Sentinel key after all other changes are written.
Call refreshOptions.RegisterAll() so that a change to any selected key-value reloads the whole configuration.
Call refreshOptions.Register("Payments:Sentinel") without refreshAll and update the sentinel key last.
Call refreshOptions.SetRefreshInterval(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30)) so that all changes are picked up together.

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Register a sentinel key with refreshAll: true and update it last.

With the sentinel key approach the provider monitors a single key. You update that key only after all other changes are complete, so the app reloads its configuration once and stays consistent. refreshAll: true makes a change to the sentinel reload all selected key-values, not just the sentinel.

RegisterAll() is incorrect for this requirement. It reloads whenever any selected key-value changes. If a refresh happens partway through the batch, the app can load a mix of old and new values.

Register without refreshAll is incorrect because only the registered key itself is reloaded when it changes. The other 20 key-values aren't refreshed.

A longer refresh interval is incorrect. It only sets the minimum time between checks and doesn't stop a refresh from landing in the middle of the batch.

References:

  • Azure App Configuration best practices
  • Tutorial: Use dynamic configuration in an ASP.NET Core app

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank runs an ASP.NET Core app in Azure App Service. The app uses its system-assigned managed identity and the App Configuration provider. It reads ordinary key-values from Azure App Configuration without problems because the identity already has the App Configuration Data Reader role.

You add a Key Vault reference named Db:Password to the store. It points to a secret in a key vault that uses the Azure RBAC permission model. The app can't resolve the secret value.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Assign the Key Vault Secrets User role on the key vault to the web app's managed identity.
In the app, call options.ConfigureKeyVault(kv => kv.SetCredential(new DefaultAzureCredential())) when adding Azure App Configuration.
Enable a managed identity on the App Configuration store and grant it the Key Vault Secrets User role on the key vault.
Replace the App Configuration Data Reader role with App Configuration Data Owner for the web app's managed identity.
Enable purge protection on the key vault.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Grant the web app's identity read access to the secret, and configure the provider's Key Vault options with a credential.

A Key Vault reference in App Configuration stores only the secret's URI. App Configuration never reads the vault: the client provider sees the reference and gets the value from Key Vault directly. The application must authenticate to both services. That means the web app's identity needs secret read access on the vault (with RBAC, Key Vault Secrets User), and the app must call ConfigureKeyVault and pass a credential through SetCredential.

Granting the App Configuration store's identity access to Key Vault is incorrect because App Configuration and Key Vault don't communicate with each other for references. The app resolves the secret.

App Configuration Data Owner is incorrect because reading key-values already works. Write permissions on the store have no effect on resolving the secret in Key Vault.

Purge protection guards against permanent deletion of the vault and its objects. It doesn't grant or affect read access.

References:

  • Tutorial: Use Key Vault references in an ASP.NET Core app

question_html:
Tailspin Toys uses Azure App Configuration feature flags with the .NET feature management library. A new checkout experience must follow these rules:

  • Always enabled for user pm@tailspintoys.com.
  • Enabled for 50 percent of users in the BetaTesters group.
  • Always disabled for members of the Contractors group.
  • Disabled for everyone else.

You need a solution that requires no custom filter code. What should you configure on the feature flag?

options.text: A targeting filter with Include Users, Include Groups (BetaTesters at 50 percent), Exclude Groups (Contractors), and a default percentage of 0
A percentage filter set to 50 percent
A time window filter with a recurrence that limits the feature to BetaTesters
Two copies of the feature flag stored under the labels BetaTesters and Contractors

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A targeting filter.

The built-in targeting filter defines an audience made of specific users, groups with their own rollout percentages, excluded users and groups, and a default percentage for everyone else. Exclusions take precedence, so Contractors are always disabled. The included user is always enabled, BetaTesters get 50 percent, and a default percentage of 0 disables the feature for all other users.

A percentage filter is incorrect because it applies one percentage to all requests. It can't include or exclude specific users or groups.

A time window filter is incorrect because it turns a feature on or off on a schedule. It has no concept of users or groups.

Copies of the flag under audience labels is incorrect because labels select which key-values the application loads, usually per environment. They don't evaluate the current user at run time, so they can't produce per-user or per-group behavior inside one app instance.

References:

  • Roll out features to targeted audiences
  • Enable features on a schedule

question_html:
Northwind Traders deploys application configuration from Azure App Configuration together with each release. The release manager needs the following:

  • The exact set of key-values that was tested in staging is the set that reaches production.
  • Nobody can change that set after it is approved.
  • If a release fails, production can return to the previous known-good configuration by changing only a single name that the app references.

What should you use?

options.text: App Configuration snapshots created with key and label filters for each release
A label per release (for example v1.4) applied to the key-values
Read-only locks on each key-value
Geo-replication of the App Configuration store to a second region

explanation_html:
Correct answer: App Configuration snapshots.

A snapshot is a named, immutable subset of a store's key-values, selected with key and label filters when it is created. Once created, its contents can't be edited. You can only archive or recover it. For a controlled rollout, the only change in the application is the name of the snapshot it references, and rollback means pointing back to the last-known-good snapshot.

A label per release is incorrect because labeled key-values are still mutable. Anyone with write access can change a v1.4 value after approval, so the set isn't guaranteed to stay the same.

Read-only locks is incorrect because they protect individual key-values but don't give you a named, versioned set to roll back to. A lock can also be removed.

Geo-replication is incorrect because it improves resiliency and spreads request load. It does nothing for versioning or immutability.

References:

  • Snapshots in Azure App Configuration
  • Azure App Configuration best practices

question_html:
Adatum stores appsettings.prod.json in an Azure Repos Git repository. A YAML pipeline uses the Azure App Configuration Import task to push the file to an App Configuration store. The task uses an Azure Resource Manager service connection with workload identity federation and Microsoft Entra authentication.

The task fails with an authorization error. You need to grant the service connection's service principal the least-privileged role that lets the task complete.

Which role should you assign on the App Configuration store?

options.text: App Configuration Data Owner
App Configuration Data Reader
Reader
Key Vault Secrets Officer

explanation_html:
Correct answer: App Configuration Data Owner.

The import task writes key-values to the store's data plane. The documented setup assigns App Configuration Data Owner to the service principal behind the service connection, which allows the task to read from and write to the store.

App Configuration Data Reader is incorrect because it allows only reading key-values, and the import task must write them.

Reader is incorrect because it is a control-plane role. With Microsoft Entra authentication, key-value data access requires one of the App Configuration data roles.

Key Vault Secrets Officer is incorrect because it grants permissions in Azure Key Vault, not in App Configuration.

References:

  • Import settings to App Configuration with Azure Pipelines

question_html:
Litware treats config/prod.json in Git as the single source of truth for production settings. A pipeline imports the file into Azure App Configuration with the Azure App Configuration Import task, using the Default file content profile, the prefix Orders:, and the label prod.

When a developer removes a setting from the file, the next pipeline run must remove the matching key-value from the store. Key-values with other prefixes or labels must not be affected.

What should you configure on the task?

options.text: Enable Delete key-values that are not included in the configuration file
Set Import Mode to Ignore-Match
Enable Dry Run
Set the File Content Profile to Kvset and leave all other options at their defaults

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Enable Delete key-values that are not included in the configuration file.

With the Default content profile, this option removes all key-values that match both the specified prefix and label before importing the file. Settings deleted from prod.json therefore disappear from the store, and key-values with other prefixes or labels aren't touched.

Ignore-Match is incorrect because it only skips key-values that already match the store. It never deletes anything.

Dry Run is incorrect because it prints the planned changes without applying them.

Kvset profile with defaults is incorrect because the delete option is unchecked by default, so nothing is removed. In addition, with Kvset the deletion scope is everything not in the file, not a prefix and label.

References:

  • Import settings to App Configuration with Azure Pipelines

question_html:
Wingtip Toys runs an Azure Functions app. The app has a system-assigned managed identity with the App Configuration Data Reader role on the store wingtip-cfg. Without changing application code, the app setting Checkout__TimeoutSeconds must take its value from the key Checkout:TimeoutSeconds with the label Production.

Which value should you assign to the app setting?

options.text: @Microsoft.AppConfiguration(Endpoint=https://wingtip-cfg.azconfig.io; Key=Checkout:TimeoutSeconds; Label=Production)
@Microsoft.KeyVault(VaultName=wingtip-cfg; SecretName=Checkout:TimeoutSeconds)
@Microsoft.AppConfiguration(SecretUri=https://wingtip-cfg.azconfig.io/kv/Checkout:TimeoutSeconds?label=Production)
$(Checkout:TimeoutSeconds@Production)

explanation_html:
Correct answer: @Microsoft.AppConfiguration(Endpoint=...; Key=...; Label=...)

App Service and Azure Functions resolve App Configuration references in application settings at the platform level, so no code change is needed. The syntax is @Microsoft.AppConfiguration({referenceString}). Endpoint and Key are required and Label is optional. The app's identity needs App Configuration Data Reader on the store, which is already in place.

@Microsoft.KeyVault(...) is incorrect because that syntax is for App Service Key Vault references and points to a key vault, not an App Configuration store.

SecretUri= is incorrect because SecretUri is a Key Vault reference parameter. App Configuration references use Endpoint, Key, and Label.

$(...) is Azure Pipelines macro syntax. App Service doesn't recognize it as a reference, so the literal string becomes the setting's value.

References:

  • Use App Configuration references for App Service and Azure Functions

question_html:
Contoso is designing a new configuration-management standard. It must cover 400 Azure virtual machines and 150 on-premises Windows and Linux servers that are onboarded to Azure Arc. Requirements:

  • Settings inside the operating system are defined as code and automatically corrected when they drift.
  • Compliance appears in Azure Policy alongside other governance results.
  • The service must remain supported for the long term.

Solution: You onboard all machines to Azure Automation State Configuration and assign node configurations that use ApplyAndAutoCorrect.

Does this meet the goal?

options.text: Yes
No

explanation_html:
Correct answer: No.

Azure Automation State Configuration is retiring on September 30, 2027, and Microsoft directs customers to Azure Machine Configuration. That fails the long-term support requirement. Its compliance also appears in Automation reports and Azure Monitor Logs, not as Azure Policy compliance.

Azure Machine Configuration combines the DSC extension and Automation State Configuration features. It audits or configures OS settings as code for Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers, and it's assigned at scale through Azure Policy. Its Apply and Autocorrect mode reapplies the configuration when drift occurs, and per-setting results appear in Azure Policy compliance and guest assignments.

References:

  • Azure Automation State Configuration overview
  • What is Azure Machine Configuration?

question_html:
Fabrikam plans to assign Azure Machine Configuration policies that apply a custom configuration to 200 Azure virtual machines in a subscription. None of the VMs currently has a managed identity or any configuration extensions.

Which two requirements must be met on each Azure VM before the guest assignments can be processed? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: The machine configuration (guest configuration) VM extension is installed.
A system-assigned managed identity is enabled on the VM.
The VM is registered as a DSC node in an Azure Automation account.
The Azure Connected Machine agent is installed on the VM.
The VM is added to a Hybrid Runbook Worker group.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: The machine configuration extension and a system-assigned managed identity.

To manage settings inside an Azure VM, the extension downloads the assigned configurations and their dependencies. The machine's system-assigned managed identity authenticates it when it reads from and writes to the machine configuration service. At scale, you deploy both by assigning the initiative Deploy prerequisites to enable Guest Configuration policies on virtual machines.

Registering as a DSC node in Automation is incorrect because that's the onboarding step for Azure Automation State Configuration, which is a separate, retiring service.

The Azure Connected Machine agent is incorrect because it's for Arc-enabled servers outside Azure. For those machines, the machine configuration capability is built into the agent, so the extension isn't needed.

A Hybrid Runbook Worker group is incorrect because it runs Automation runbooks and has no role in machine configuration.

References:

  • Azure Machine Configuration prerequisites

question_html:
Adatum uses Azure Machine Configuration to set registry-based hardening settings on application servers. The application team sometimes changes these settings during troubleshooting. Requirements:

  • Apply the configuration to each server.
  • If a server later drifts, report it as NonCompliant.
  • Do not automatically revert the change. Remediation must be triggered deliberately.

Which assignment type should you use?

options.text: ApplyAndMonitor
ApplyAndAutoCorrect
Audit
ApplyOnly

explanation_html:
Correct answer: ApplyAndMonitor

ApplyAndMonitor applies the configuration to the machine once and then monitors it. If the configuration drifts, the guest assignment reports NonCompliant, but nothing is corrected until remediation is triggered.

ApplyAndAutoCorrect is incorrect because the local agent corrects drift at the next evaluation. That conflicts with the requirement not to revert changes automatically.

Audit is incorrect because it only reports on the machine's state and never applies the configuration.

ApplyOnly is a configuration mode of the PowerShell DSC Local Configuration Manager, not a machine configuration assignment type. The valid assignment types are Audit, ApplyAndMonitor, and ApplyAndAutoCorrect.

References:

  • Remediation options for machine configuration

question_html:
You are building custom content for Azure Machine Configuration. You compiled a PowerShell DSC configuration and renamed the output to ./WebBaseline/WebBaseline.mof. Next you must produce the .zip artifact that will be uploaded to storage and referenced by a policy definition. The package must apply the settings, not only audit them.

$params = @{
    Name          = 'WebBaseline'
    Configuration = './WebBaseline/WebBaseline.mof'
    Type          = 'AuditAndSet'
    Force         = $true
}
SLOT_1 @params

Which cmdlet should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: New-GuestConfigurationPackage
New-GuestConfigurationPolicy
Import-AzAutomationDscConfiguration
Publish-AzVMDscConfiguration

explanation_html:
Correct answer: New-GuestConfigurationPackage

After the MOF is compiled, New-GuestConfigurationPackage from the GuestConfiguration module bundles the MOF, the required DSC resource modules, and a metaconfig into a .zip package. Its parameters include Name, Configuration (the MOF path), and Type. Use Audit to only audit or AuditAndSet to also apply the configuration.

New-GuestConfigurationPolicy is incorrect at this step. It runs after the package is published: it takes the package's ContentUri and generates the Azure Policy definition. It doesn't accept a MOF or a Type parameter.

Import-AzAutomationDscConfiguration is incorrect because it imports a configuration into Azure Automation State Configuration, not machine configuration.

Publish-AzVMDscConfiguration is incorrect because it packages a configuration for the Azure DSC VM extension, not for machine configuration.

References:

  • How to create custom machine configuration package artifacts
  • How to create custom machine configuration policy definitions

question_html:
Tailspin Toys manages its Azure infrastructure with Terraform. State is stored remotely in Azure Storage. Engineers sometimes change resources directly in the Azure portal. You need a nightly scheduled pipeline that detects configuration drift between the Terraform configuration and the real infrastructure and alerts the team. It must not change any resources.

Solution: The pipeline runs terraform init and then terraform plan -detailed-exitcode. If the command returns exit code 2, a later step raises an alert.

Does this meet the goal?

options.text: Yes
No

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Yes.

terraform plan refreshes state against the real infrastructure and computes a diff without changing any resources. With -detailed-exitcode, it returns 0 when there is no diff, 1 on error, and 2 when changes are present. On a schedule, exit code 2 means the real infrastructure no longer matches the configuration (drift), and the pipeline can use it to raise an alert.

Without -detailed-exitcode, a successful plan returns 0 whether or not there are changes, so the pipeline couldn't tell drift from no drift. Running terraform apply wouldn't meet the goal because it changes resources.

References:

  • Terraform CLI: terraform plan command

question_html:
Contoso's release pipeline runs Ansible playbooks against Azure VMs. To avoid maintaining a static hosts file, an engineer creates the following file named inventory.yml:

plugin: azure_rm
include_vm_resource_groups:
  - rg-web-prod
auth_source: auto
keyed_groups:
  - key: tags.applicationRole

Running ansible-inventory -i inventory.yml --graph doesn't use the Azure dynamic inventory plug-in, and no VMs are returned.

What should you do?

options.text: Rename the file so that its name ends with azure_rm.yml, for example web.azure_rm.yml.
Replace keyed_groups with conditional_groups.
Add plain_host_names: yes to the file.
Install the pywinrm Python package on the agent.

explanation_html:
Correct answer: Rename the file so that it ends with azure_rm.yml (or azure_rm.yaml).

Ansible uses the inventory file name and extension to decide which inventory plug-in to use. To use the Azure dynamic inventory plug-in, the file name must end with azure_rm and have a yml or yaml extension, for example myazure_rm.yml. A generic inventory.yml isn't recognized as an Azure dynamic inventory.

conditional_groups is incorrect because grouping options only take effect once the plug-in runs. Keyed groups by tag are valid.

plain_host_names is incorrect because it only removes the unique suffix from host names in the output.

pywinrm is incorrect because it is needed to connect to Windows hosts over WinRM. It has nothing to do with building the inventory.

References:

  • Tutorial: Configure dynamic inventories for Azure Virtual Machines using Ansible

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank has one YAML pipeline that deploys to dev, test, or prod. Each environment has a variables template file (vars/dev.yml, vars/test.yml, vars/prod.yml). When an engineer manually runs the pipeline:

  • They must choose the target from a drop-down that allows only those three values.
  • The choice must decide, at pipeline compile time, which variables template is included through a ${{ if }} template expression.
  • The value can't be changed after the run is queued.

What should you define?

options.text: A runtime parameter of type string with a values list of dev, test, and prod
A pipeline variable with the Let users override this value when running this pipeline option enabled
A variable group linked to the pipeline that contains an Environment variable
A variable set with runtime expression syntax $[ ] that reads Build.Reason

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A runtime parameter with a values list.

Runtime parameters have a data type and can be limited to a list of allowed values, which appear in the Run pipeline pane. They're expanded during template parsing, before the run starts. That makes them available to ${{ }} template expressions such as conditional insertion of a variables template. After the run is queued, they can't be changed.

A queue-time overridable variable is incorrect because the user can type any value, and template expressions can't see values supplied when a run starts. Only variables defined in the YAML and some predefined variables are available at template expansion.

A variable group is incorrect because it doesn't give a restricted choice at queue time. Its values aren't available to template expressions at compile time either.

A runtime expression $[ ] is incorrect because it's evaluated after template expansion, when a job or stage starts. It's too late to decide which template is included, and it offers no drop-down.

References:

  • Use runtime and type-safe parameters
  • Template expressions

question_html:
Northwind Traders replaces its JSON parameter files with Bicep parameter files. The file main.prod.bicepparam must be linked to main.bicep in the same folder, so that the pipeline can deploy with only:

az deployment group create \
  --resource-group rg-app-prod \
  --parameters main.prod.bicepparam

The parameter file is:

SLOT_1

param appServicePlanSku = 'P1v3'
param instanceCount = 3

What should you use for SLOT_1?

options.text: using './main.bicep'
extends './main.bicep'
import './main.bicep'
targetScope = 'resourceGroup'

explanation_html:
Correct answer: using './main.bicep'

The using statement links a .bicepparam file to its Bicep file. With that link, Azure CLI 2.53.0 or later can deploy by passing only the .bicepparam file to --parameters, without a --template-file switch. Tooling also uses the link to validate parameter names and types.

extends is incorrect because it inherits parameter values from a base .bicepparam file. It doesn't reference the Bicep template.

import is incorrect because import {...} from brings exported types, variables, or functions into a file. It doesn't link a template for deployment, and the shown form isn't valid import syntax.

targetScope is incorrect because it's a Bicep template statement that declares the deployment scope. It isn't valid in a parameters file.

References:

  • Create parameters files for Bicep deployment

question_html:
An engineer at Litware deploys Bicep files to a resource group from the Azure CLI. Before each deployment, they must see which resources will be created, modified, or deleted, and then be prompted to continue or cancel. They want to do this with a single command.

Which command should they run?

options.text: az deployment group create --resource-group rg-litware --template-file main.bicep --confirm-with-what-if
az deployment group what-if --resource-group rg-litware --template-file main.bicep
az deployment group validate --resource-group rg-litware --template-file main.bicep
az deployment group create --resource-group rg-litware --template-file main.bicep --mode Complete

explanation_html:
Correct answer: az deployment group create ... --confirm-with-what-if (short form -c)

The --confirm-with-what-if switch runs the what-if operation, shows the predicted changes, and then asks whether to continue with the deployment. Both requirements are met in one command.

az deployment group what-if is incorrect because it only previews changes. A second create command is still needed to deploy.

az deployment group validate is incorrect because it checks that the template is valid and would be accepted, but it doesn't list per-resource changes or deploy.

--mode Complete is incorrect because it changes deployment behavior so resources not in the template are deleted. It doesn't preview or prompt.

References:

  • Bicep what-if: Preview changes before deployment

question_html:
Resource group rg-tailspin contains resources A, B, C, and E. You deploy an ARM JSON template with the latest Azure CLI by using az deployment group create --mode Complete. The template defines:

  • Resources A and B (unchanged)
  • A new resource D
  • Resource E, with a condition that evaluates to false for this deployment

The resource group has no locks, and all resource types support complete-mode deletion. Which resources exist in the resource group after the deployment?

options.text: A, B, and D
A, B, D, and E
A, B, C, D, and E
A, B, C, and D

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A, B, and D.

In complete mode, Resource Manager deletes resources in the resource group that aren't specified in the template, so C is deleted. If a resource in the template isn't deployed because its condition evaluates to false, deployments that use REST API version 2019-05-10 or later delete it, and the latest Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell use such versions. E is therefore deleted too. D is created, and A and B remain.

A, B, D, and E is incorrect because a false condition doesn't protect an existing resource in complete mode with current API versions. This was only true for API versions earlier than 2019-05-10.

A, B, C, D, and E describes incremental mode, which leaves resources that aren't in the template unchanged.

A, B, C, and D is incorrect because C isn't in the template and is deleted, while E is deleted for the reason above.

Microsoft recommends previewing complete-mode deployments with what-if. It also notes that complete mode is being gradually deprecated in favor of deployment stacks for deletions.

References:

  • Azure Resource Manager deployment modes

question_html:
Fabrikam deploys a Bicep file to resource group rg-shared with az stack group create. Requirements:

  • When a resource definition is removed from the Bicep file, the next stack update must delete that resource from Azure. Resource groups must not be deleted.
  • Users must not be able to delete stack-managed resources outside the stack, but operators must still be able to change settings on them, such as scaling an App Service plan.

Which two parameter values should you specify? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: --action-on-unmanage deleteResources
--deny-settings-mode denyDelete
--action-on-unmanage detachAll
--deny-settings-mode denyWriteAndDelete
--mode Complete

explanation_html:
Correct answers: --action-on-unmanage deleteResources and --deny-settings-mode denyDelete

action-on-unmanage controls what happens to resources that are no longer in the template. deleteResources deletes the unmanaged resources but not resource groups, while deleteAll would also delete resource groups. deny-settings-mode denyDelete creates a deny assignment that blocks delete operations on managed resources but still allows write (update) operations.

detachAll is incorrect because removed resources are only detached from the stack and keep running. This is the default behavior.

denyWriteAndDelete is incorrect because it also blocks updates, so operators couldn't scale the App Service plan.

--mode Complete is incorrect because it's a deployment-mode option of az deployment group create, not of deployment stacks. Microsoft recommends deployment stacks instead of complete mode for deletions.

References:

  • Create and deploy Azure deployment stacks in Bicep
  • Azure Resource Manager deployment modes

question_html:
Adatum needs one Bicep file that creates a resource group and then deploys a storage module into that new resource group. It is deployed with az deployment sub create.

targetScope = 'subscription'

param location string = deployment().location

resource newRG 'Microsoft.Resources/resourceGroups@2025-04-01' = {
  name: 'rg-adatum-data'
  location: location
}

module stg './storage.bicep' = {
  name: 'storageDeploy'
  scope: SLOT_1
  params: {
    location: location
  }
}

What should you use for SLOT_1 so that the module deploys into the new resource group and waits for it to be created?

options.text: newRG
resourceGroup()
subscription()
'rg-adatum-data'

explanation_html:
Correct answer: newRG

When a subscription-scope Bicep file creates a resource group, you set a module's scope to that resource group's symbolic name. That targets the module at the new resource group and creates an implicit dependency, so the module is deployed only after the resource group exists.

resourceGroup() without arguments is incorrect because it returns the current deployment's resource group, and a subscription-scope deployment has none. To target an existing group by name you would use resourceGroup('name'), which doesn't create a dependency on the resource being created here.

subscription() is incorrect because it scopes the module to the subscription, not to the resource group.

A string literal is incorrect because scope requires a scope object, either a symbolic name or the result of a scope function. A plain string isn't valid.

References:

  • Use Bicep to deploy resources to subscription
  • Bicep modules

question_html:
Contoso's platform team maintains a hardened, versioned template for an App Service landing zone. Application teams must deploy it:

  • from the Azure portal and from Azure CLI scripts,
  • without access to the platform team's Git repository and without SAS tokens,
  • with access controlled through Azure RBAC, so that application teams can deploy the template but not modify it.

What should the platform team publish the template as?

options.text: A template spec, with the Template Spec Reader role granted to the application teams
A module in a private Bicep registry hosted in Azure Container Registry, with the AcrPull role granted to the application teams
A JSON file in a blob container in Azure Storage that application teams access through a SAS URI
An Azure Verified Module referenced through the br/public alias

explanation_html:
Correct answer: A template spec.

A template spec stores an ARM template (Bicep is transpiled) as an Azure resource. Access is managed with Azure RBAC, and users need only read access, for example through Template Spec Reader, to deploy it without being able to modify it. Template specs support versions and can be deployed directly from the Azure portal, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, and the REST API.

A private Bicep registry module is incorrect because registry content can be deployed only from another Bicep file. It can't be deployed directly from the Azure portal.

A blob with a SAS URI is incorrect because it explicitly violates the no-SAS requirement and doesn't provide RBAC-based sharing.

An Azure Verified Module through br/public is incorrect because the public registry holds Microsoft-owned modules. The platform team can't publish its own private template there.

References:

  • Create and deploy template specs in Bicep
  • Bicep modules

question_html:
Wingtip Toys published a Bicep module to its private registry with this command:

az bicep publish --file keyvault.bicep \
  --target br:wingtipiac.azurecr.io/bicep/modules/keyvault:v2

No module aliases are configured in bicepconfig.json. You need to consume the module from another Bicep file.

module kv 'SLOT_1' = {
  params: {
    vaultName: 'kv-wingtip-prod'
  }
}

What should you use for SLOT_1?
