options.text: br:wingtipiac.azurecr.io/bicep/modules/keyvault:v2
br/public:bicep/modules/keyvault:v2
ts:wingtipiac.azurecr.io/bicep/modules/keyvault:v2
oci://wingtipiac.azurecr.io/bicep/modules/keyvault@v2

explanation_html:
Correct answer: br:wingtipiac.azurecr.io/bicep/modules/keyvault:v2

Modules in a private Bicep registry, which is hosted in Azure Container Registry, are referenced with the br: scheme, followed by <registry>.azurecr.io/<repository-path>:<tag>. This is the same value that was used as the publish target. Without an alias, you must use the full path. The module name property is optional.

br/public: is incorrect because it's the predefined alias for the public module registry (Azure Verified Modules on mcr.microsoft.com), not Wingtip's private registry.

ts: is incorrect because it references a template spec, using the format ts:<sub-id>/<rg>/<name>:<version>, not a container registry.

oci:// is incorrect because Bicep module paths don't support that scheme or the @ version form.

References:

  • Bicep modules
  • Create a private container registry in Azure for Bicep modules

question_html:
Several Azure Pipelines and engineers run Terraform against the same configuration. The state is stored remotely with this backend:

terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    resource_group_name  = "rg-tfstate"
    storage_account_name = "sttfstatecontoso"
    container_name       = "tfstate"
    key                  = "prod.terraform.tfstate"
    use_azuread_auth     = true
  }
}

You must prevent two runs from writing the state file at the same time, regardless of which pipeline or user starts them, with the least administrative effort. What should you do?

options.text: Nothing additional. The azurerm backend automatically locks the state blob by using Azure Blob Storage native capabilities before any operation that writes state.
Create an Azure Cosmos DB table for locks and reference it in the backend block.
Enable blob versioning and soft delete on the tfstate container.
Add an Exclusive lock check to the production environment in Azure Pipelines.

explanation_html:
Correct answer: No extra configuration is required.

The azurerm backend supports state locking and consistency checking with Azure Blob Storage native capabilities. The state blob is locked automatically before any operation that writes state, which blocks concurrent operations from any client, including pipelines and engineers' workstations.

A separate lock table is incorrect because that pattern belongs to other backends, such as an Amazon DynamoDB table for the S3 backend. The azurerm backend has no such setting.

Blob versioning and soft delete help you recover an overwritten or deleted state file, but they don't stop concurrent writes.

An Exclusive lock check serializes pipeline stages that use that Azure Pipelines resource. It doesn't protect against engineers or other pipelines running Terraform outside that environment, and it adds administration that isn't needed.

References:

  • Store Terraform state in Azure Storage
  • Terraform backend type: azurerm

question_html:
Tailspin Toys uses a multi-stage YAML pipeline in Azure Pipelines to deploy Terraform. Requirements:

  • A reviewer approves the exact changes produced by terraform plan. The apply stage must apply exactly that reviewed plan, even if the configuration or the infrastructure changes in the meantime.
  • The approval is controlled by the owners of the production target and can't be removed by someone who edits the pipeline YAML.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: In the plan stage, run terraform plan -out=tfplan and publish tfplan as a pipeline artifact. In the apply stage, download it and run terraform apply tfplan.
Run the apply stage as a deployment job that targets an Azure Pipelines environment named prod, and add an Approvals check to that environment.
In the apply stage, run terraform apply -auto-approve against the checked-out configuration.
Add a ManualValidation@1 task to an agentless job at the start of the apply stage.
In the plan stage, run terraform plan -refresh-only and require the reviewer to approve its output.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Save the plan file and apply it, and gate the apply stage with an Approvals check on an environment.

When you pass a saved plan file from terraform plan -out=FILE to terraform apply, Terraform performs exactly that plan instead of generating a new one. The reviewed changes are the applied changes. Plan files can contain sensitive values in cleartext, so protect the artifact.

Approvals and checks are defined on protected resources such as environments by the resource owners in the Azure Pipelines web UI, not in YAML. A deployment job that targets the environment pauses until the approval is granted, and editing the YAML can't remove the check.

terraform apply -auto-approve on the configuration is incorrect because it computes a fresh plan at apply time, which might differ from the reviewed plan.

ManualValidation@1 is incorrect for this requirement because the task is defined in the YAML. Anyone who edits the pipeline can remove or change it, so it isn't controlled by the target's owners.

-refresh-only is incorrect because it only plans updates to state from the real infrastructure. It doesn't show the configuration changes that apply would make.

References:

  • Terraform CLI: terraform plan command
  • Pipeline deployment approvals

question_html:
Woodgrove Bank runs Terraform with the AzureRM provider from a GitHub Actions workflow. Security policy forbids storing client secrets or storage access keys in GitHub. A Microsoft Entra app registration has a federated credential that trusts the repository's production environment. The repository secrets AZURE_CLIENT_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID, and AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID are mapped to ARM_CLIENT_ID, ARM_TENANT_ID, and ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID.

The terraform plan step fails to authenticate. Which two changes should you make to the workflow? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

options.text: Add permissions with id-token: write (and contents: read) to the workflow or job.
Set the environment variable ARM_USE_OIDC to true for the Terraform steps.
Add a repository secret named ARM_CLIENT_SECRET and map it to the Terraform steps.
Set ARM_ACCESS_KEY to the state storage account key retrieved in a previous step.
Add permissions with contents: write to the job.

explanation_html:
Correct answers: Grant id-token: write and set ARM_USE_OIDC=true.

For a workflow to request an OIDC token from GitHub, the job needs permissions: id-token: write. This permission lets the job request and use the token, but it doesn't let the job modify resources. The AzureRM provider uses workload identity federation (OIDC) when ARM_USE_OIDC is set to true together with ARM_CLIENT_ID, ARM_TENANT_ID, and ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID. The azurerm backend can use OIDC in the same way (use_oidc).

ARM_CLIENT_SECRET is incorrect because it's secret-based service principal authentication, which the policy forbids.

ARM_ACCESS_KEY is incorrect because it authenticates to the state storage account with a shared key, which is also a stored credential. It doesn't fix provider authentication either.

contents: write is incorrect because it lets the job push to the repository and has nothing to do with obtaining an OIDC token.

References:

  • Configuring OpenID Connect in Azure
  • AzureRM provider: Authenticating using a service principal and OpenID Connect
